items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: When the House resumes on
Tuesday, 17 March the Government will look to progress a number of bills on the Order
Paper, including the Human Rights Amendment Bill, the Construction Contracts
Amendment Bill, and the Statutes Amendment Bill (No 4).

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I wonder whether the Leader of the
House could advise us whether the Government has any intentions to progress matters
regarding members’ remuneration during next week and whether in fact he envisages
that replacing the members’ day that would normally be scheduled for Wednesday.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: It is most definitely the
Government’s intention to progress that legislation. It is not the Government’s intention
for it to impede members’ day.
Prime Minister—Northland By-election
1. RON MARK (NZ First)  to the Prime Minister: Does he stand by all his
statements?
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister)  on behalf of the  Prime Minister:
Yes.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Given that the Prime Minister said “last week we were looking through
the various policies we want to announce —so they were finalised, I suppose, last
week.”, on what date and at what time, then, was the decision taken to double -lane the
eight Northland bridges not listed in the draf t Northland regional land transport plan

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I cannot give exactly that detail, other than to say it was
before it was announced. But it is certainly the Government’s plan to campaign on what
it plans to do for Nort hland. The issue for New Zealand First is whether or not it is for
or against the bridges being double-laned.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My colleague Tracey Martin
yesterday asked this very question. It has been 24 hours sinc e that question was put. We
would have thought that by this stage the Prime  Minister’s office might be  able to give
you that answer—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I refer the member to the primary question he has
asked: “Does the Prime Minister stand by all his statements?”. Then he asked a
supplementary question that said: “On what particular date and at what time was this
decision made?”. The Minister is quite at liberty to say, when he rises to answer that
question, that he does not have that information with him.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Since the 3 News  Reid Research Services poll of 5 March 2015, what is
the cumulative value of policy pledges made by Ministers to Northland?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think that National Party policy is the one that has been
announced, because we are campaigning to get an MP into Parliament who represents
Northland, not one who represents Southland.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! This is a point of order.
2202 Oral Questions  12 Mar 2015

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: The question was nothing to do about what the National Party is
campaigning to do; it was about the value of—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is now making exactly the same point as he
made just befo re. If he asks a very general primary question, such as “Does the Prime
Minister stand by all his statements?”, and then he moves on to ask quite specific
supplementary questions about a cumulative dollar value, he cannot expect the Minister
to have that information with him. Does the member wish to ask further supplementary
questions or shall we move to question No. 2?

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Further to the Prime Minister’s points of order yesterday, are the pledges
he is making to the people of Northland being made in his capacity as the Prime
Minister or as the leader of a very nervous National Party?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There is no responsibility for the Prime Minister’s role as
leader of the National Party, but I can say that they are pr omises made out of respect for
the voters of Northland, who need to know what they are voting for, not what they are
voting against. Part of the plan is to get an MP who will service Northland, not a new
New Zealand First MP from Invercargill, which is wha t that member is campaigning
for.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Then how many Ministers have visited Northland since 5 March, and
what specific ministerial duties have they been performing whilst they are up there?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: If the member spent more time up there and not trying to
elect an MP from Southland for Northland, he would know. There have been quite a
few ministerial visits, because the Government does a lot in Northland and it plans to do
a lot more. And we believe that Northland voters deserve to see what the plan is.
Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus and Ministerial Responsibility
2. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: Does he stand by his statement “every Minister believes that the decision that
affects them is the one that makes all the difference to the surplus or the deficit”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I do, because I am sure there are
any number of Ministers who believe that their decisions or decisions about their
portfolio were responsible for the fact that Treasury announced in the 7 months to
January a $77 mi llion surplus, the first one in a number of years. Of course, it is too
early to tell whether that will translate into a surplus for the full year, but we are quite
happy for any and every Minister to claim credit for the fiscal management that has
gone into generating that $77 million surplus.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does every Minister have advice from their own department,
Treasury, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, and outside agencies
that they are in a position to save Ne w Zealand businesses and workers $350 million, as
the Minister for ACC had?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: All I say to that member is that when those members
attacked the manufacturing sector by saying it was in crisis, it came right, and now that
they are attacking the surplus, we have got one.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Can I invite the member to repeat his question.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Do not interrupt him this time, Gerry—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I have been gracious enough to the
member to allow him to ask his question. I would now be grateful if he would.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does every Minister have advice from their o wn department,
Treasury, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, and outside agencies
that they are in a position to save New Zealand businesses and workers $350 million, as
the Minister for ACC had?
12 Mar 2015 Oral Questions  2203

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, but  I think that a number of Ministers have had advice
that protests outside Government agencies over restructuring and excessive wage rises
would probably make it harder to get to the surplus, and that member has organised
such—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! The question was answered at the very
start.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Has the Minister of Revenue expressed the belief to him that
decisions around the implementation of the child support system will make the
difference between surplus and deficit, given that the cost of that project had blown out
from $30 million to $210 million?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think he may have done and, as I think has been discussed
both here and in the select committee, the child support changes were made a great deal
more complex by the select committee. It turns out that the cost of inserting those more
complex changes into a very old tax system were high, and the Minister took a number
of policy decisions to wind them back and r educe the cost, and that has helped us get to
a surplus.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How often did the Minister of Revenue report to him about the
escalation of $180 million of cost on the implementation of the child support system?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Oh, pretty regularly over a period of 2 or 3 years. I mean, it
is a large, complex area of policy, where striking a balance between administrative cost
and fairness has proven to be very difficult. Every member of this House gets to dea l
with people who feel like they are on the wrong end of the child support law, and I
thought that the member might have been a bit more understanding about the reality for
many New Zealand families.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: As Minister of Finance, has he sought to hold anyone accountable
for a blowout of $180 million in the implementation of the child support system?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes. There have been a lot of discussions about clarity and
accountability, and I think, as the Commissioner of Inland Revenue has stated in the last
few days, ultimately she is accountable.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: If she is accountable, what action does the Government intend to
take?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, the Government has a lot of confidence, actually, in
the Commissioner of Inland Revenue. It has taken a series of decisions to minimise the
cost and, actually, if the member took the time to understand the issues involved, he
would probably be asking a different set of questions.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: So can we confirm for the House’s benefit that the Minister of
Finance does not believe that he needs to do anything in particular about the fact that
there has been a $180 million blowout in the cost  of implementing the child support
system?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I would not confirm that, because it is not the case. The
Government has worked on this issue for 3, if not 4, years, trying to deal with the
complexity and cost of deliveri ng more fairness for New Zealand families who find
themselves in pretty difficult situations, and I think that every member of Parliament
knows how hard these issues are. It turned out to cost more than was originally
expected. A number of decisions were taken to wind that cost back considerably.
Monetary Policy Statement—March 2015 Forecasts
3. Dr JIAN YANG (National)  to the Minister of Finance: What recent reports has
he received about the growth outlook for the New Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Today the Reserve Bank issued its
Monetary Policy Statement for March with updated forecasts that the economy will
2204 Oral Questions  12 Mar 2015
grow by 3 to 4 percent over each of the next 2 years, after estimated growth of over 3
percent in 2014. The bank says that the domestic economy remains strong supported by
growth in employment and construction activity. Business investment and household
income and consumption are moderately strong, supported by low interest rates, high
net migration, rising house prices, and the flow -on effects of high commodity export
prices in the last dairy season. As the Reserve Bank pointed out, of course there are
some risks to this scenario over the next couple of years. It also forecast that annual
inflation to March 2015 would be zero, which I think is unprecedented, and revised
down its estimates of increases in the cost of living to 1.3 percent for the year to Mar ch

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: What does the Reserve Bank see as the main drivers of inflation and
the economic outlook?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Reserve Bank says that headline inflation forecasts
reflect a high exchange rate, weak global inflation, and falling oil prices, so, effectively,
New Zealand is importing deflation from offshore. Domestic or non-tradable inflation is
higher at 2.4 percent but it does remain well below the long -term average. Oil prices are
expected to remain at their current level over the next 2 years, moderating tradables
inflation and boosting incomes and economic activity. The Reserve Bank says the
outlook for the economy depends on these four factors: oil prices, dairy prices and
farmers’ spending, domestic capacity pressures, and the housing market.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: What is the role of housing in the outlook from the Reserve Bank?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Reserve Bank seems to spend a lot of time focusing on
the housing market be cause in an economy where most things seem to be pointing
towards sustained economic growth for some time, which will lift incomes and
households across the country, the housing market in Auckland is one obvious
imbalance. Projected building work continues  to rise with the Canterbury rebuild, and
building work continues to rise in response to the housing shortage in Auckland. House
price inflation is being driven in part by net migration and by falling interest rates, but
also the Reserve Bank agrees with t he Government’s view that shortage of supply is a
critical driver of house price increases in Auckland.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: What steps is the Government taking to improve housing supply and
take pressure off interest rates?

items.speaker: Hon B ILL ENGLISH
items.text: Of course, the critical thing about housing supply to
understand is that it is councils that make the decisions. So the Government is working
closely with councils to create special housing areas; we are reforming the Resource
Management Act, which I know will have support from the Opposition members who
are keen to see the supply of housing expanded; and we are spending $1.9 billion a year
on accommodation support. On 1 April the Government’s KiwiSaver HomeStart
programme will get under way, and that will also encourage new supply of housing.
Roading, Northland—Spending
4. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour —Te Atatū) to the Minister of Transport : How
much has been spent in total by the New Zealand Transport Agency on roads in the
Northland region under National Land Transport Programmes set by the current
Government since it was elected in November 2008?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I cannot be as precise as the
member seeks, because records on spending are kept only year on year and start in July
and finish in June the following year. But starting in July 2008 through to June 2015
this Government has spent $750 million on Northland roads, some 40 percent more than
the Labour Government did in the same period of time. We back Northland, unlike the
Labour Party and New Zealand First.
12 Mar 2015 Oral Questions  2205

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question w as on notice. The
National Land Transport Programme provides detailed information on yearly
disbursements. It is not good enough for the Minister to say he cannot answer that
question in detail or accurately.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, no. As I understood the Minister, he then talked about
the financial year, so he gave a figure from 1 July 2008 of $750 million. The question
has undoubtedly been addressed. If the member feels it is an unreasonable answer, I
suggest he now makes progress with his supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: When he told the media and the House that National had spent $750
million on Northland roads, was he aware that that includes a quarter of a billion dollars
budgeted or spent by the then Labour Government; if so, why is he trying to deceive the
people of this country about his cuts to the road funding in Northland?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Simon Bridges—either of those supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: The member is p lain, simple wrong. We have spent $750
million over 7 years. But here is the thing, Mr Twyford: no matter how you cut the
numbers, year on year, month on month, we have spent more than you.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is not—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am on my feet.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Yes, Mr Speaker. I see that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am on my feet.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Would you like me to sit down?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I would like that. I was going to say to the Minister that it is not
appropriate to bring the Speaker into this debate.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: If the Minister quoted from an official document when he gave
the figures to the House today, could he please table it? I am waiting for—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is easily resolved. Did the Minister quote  from an official
document? [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Why is he refusing to release the cost -benefit analyses completed for
each of the 10 new bridges, and which projects have been cut or delayed to free up the
funding for his by-election announcement?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Again, either of those two supplementary questions, the Hon Simon
Bridges.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I appreciate it is difficult for the member. This is the
second question he has asked me, ever —some 200 percent in 1 week—so I say
congratulations on asking a question. The proje cts stack up. There are three bridges that
will be prioritised in the first 3 years. All are in the regional land transport plan. It is
quite clear to the people of Northland that these are important projects that need to be
done, and we back Northland.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Was he aware, when planning to widen—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member can start his question again.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Was he aware, when planning to widen  the “Darby and Joan” kauri
bridge in Waipoua Forest that it is not actually a bridge but a single -lane section of road
left that way in order to protect two ancient kauri trees? What does this Government
have against ancient kauri trees —first the Resource Management Act reforms, and now
they are in the way of National’s pork barrel?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Again, the Hon Simon Bridges —either of those two supplementary
questions.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I can assure the member that “Darby and Joan” are safe
and sound.
2206 Oral Questions  12 Mar 2015

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Had he seen the widely published photograph of his colleagues
putting up an election hoarding close to a busy main road before he announced—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! There is no ministerial responsibility in that question.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The ministerial responsibility lies
in the fact that the question—you did not listen to the full question—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat. He is very lucky that he is
remaining in the Chamber today. I have ruled that question out of order. I will on this
occasion give the member the opportunity to have another question, otherwise we are
moving on.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Has he been advised that the widely published photograph of his
colleagues putting up an election hoarding  was done before his announcement of the 10
new bridges in Northland; if  so, is he embarrassed that local people are taking the large
pig standing in the photograph as a metaphor for his announcement?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I fail to see much ministerial responsibility. I will leave it for the
Minister to answer. I call the H on Simon Bridges, but he has a certain amount of
latitude.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I understand the anger and disappointment from the
member opposite. It must be gutting to know—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will r emove that sign immediately from the
Chamber. The member will remove that from the Chamber. Does the Minister wish to
complete his answer?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I appreciate it is gutting—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Because of the way that was taken from the Chamber, the
member can remove himself for the balance of question time.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, first of all I want the member to remove himself.
Phil Twyford withdrew from the Chamber.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order. It will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: There are some quite clear Speakers’ rulings around the use of props
in the  House, and I wonder whether you could indicate for future reference, so that
members can comply with those, which of those you feel Mr Twyford did not comply
with.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I can. If the member wants to look at Speakers’ rulings 56 and 57,
there are a number of rulings about the use of visual aids. If they are of value to the
House, then they can be used. That one I determined was straight electioneering and
under no circumstances will I allow that. [ Interruption] Order! Under no circumstances
will I allow that to be displayed in this Chamber. Then I asked the member to remove it.
The way he then removed it, by displaying it to everybody in this House, I found totally
unacceptable. On that basis I have asked the member to leave the Chamber.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is it a relitigation?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: No, not at all. I wish to table the New Zealand Transport
Agency figures from 2007-08, 2008-09, to 2013-14 showing that—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has explained what she is attempting to table. I
just need to check whether the information is freely available on the website.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Yes, it is, and I will not —[Interruption] If other people wish to
leave and accompany their colleague, I can assist.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Can I jus t clarify because
the Minister said they were not available—
12 Mar 2015 Oral Questions  2207

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is really testing my patience. I have explained
on many occasions the purpose of tabling a document. It is not to make a political point.
It is to furthe r inform the proceedings of the House. On this occasion, I have ruled that
if it is freely available to members, they have the ability after question time to go back
and, if they want that information, get it on the website. Members need to bear in mind
the tabling of documents is not to make a political point.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: Can the Minister confirm, according to advice from his own
officials, that funding ranges for local roads, road maintenance, and road safety were
reduced by Nat ional in 2009 and 2012 in order to increase funding ranges for a few
expensive new State highways, none of which are in Northland?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: That is incorrect. I appreciate, though, the member’s
interest in public transport. We  have not made an announcement on that in Northland
yet. Can I say we have not talked about buses. That is lucky, though, because that is
what the Labour Party, through—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That will not help the order of this House. [ Interruption]
Order! I will be asking somebody to leave, and it will be from the front bench on my
left at this stage.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: I seek leave to table this report from the Ministry of Transport
stating that funding ranges for new and improved State highways were significantly
increased in 2009 and 2012—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The document has been described. I just again need to check
the source. Is it freely available to members on the web?

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: No, it was not.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will take the member’s word and therefore put the leave. It is a
Ministry of Transport report that is not freely available to members. I am putting the
leave. The House can decide. Is there any objection to that be ing tabled? There is not. It
can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Independent Police Conduct Authority—Iriheke Pere Case
5. MARAMA FOX (Co -Leader—Māori Party)  to the Minister of Police: What
advice, if any, has he received about Iriheke Pere given that it is over 18 months since
he was shot in the back while he was handcuffed and not resisting arrest?
Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Associate Minister of Justice)  on behalf of the Minister
of Justice: I appreciate the member’s interest in the matter. Of course, it is the subject
of an Independent Police Conduct Authority inquiry . The authority is independent in its
day-to-day operations and it does not report to the Minister of Justice on individual
complaints, so I have not received any advice on the matter.

items.speaker: Marama Fox
items.text: Although we acknowledge that the Independent P olice Conduct
Authority is an independent authority, we would like to know whether the Minister has
any indication of when Iriheke Pere and his whānau expect to receive a report
explaining why he was shot.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: As the member acknowledges, the Independent Police
Conduct Authority is independent in its operations and it would not be appropriate for
me to comment on a specific case. The member will, if she has a strong interest in it—
and I am sure she does—need to take this particular matter up with the authority.

items.speaker: Marama Fox
items.text: What assurances can the Minister give that the delay in the timing of
the report will not impact on Iriheke Pere’s potential claim for personal injury, given
that the statute of limitations for personal injuries ends in August 2015?
2208 Oral Questions  12 Mar 2015

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: As I say, the Independent Police Conduct Authority is
independent. I think that given the tenor of the member’s question it is a matter on
which Iriheke Pere would be wise to take legal advice.
Roading, Waikato—Waikato Expressway
6. DAVID BENNETT (National —Hamilton East) to the Minister of Transport :
What progress has the Government made on completing the Wai kato Expressway Road
of National Significance?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Earlier this week I was delighted
to announce that over $1 billion worth of funding has  been approved by the New
Zealand Transport Agency for work to complete the remaining three sections of the
Waikato Expressway. The funding means that planning and work on the final three
sections of this motorway can get under way, which, when completed, will see the
expressway extend 102 kilometres from Cambridge to the base of the Bombay Hills.
The new funding will also bring the Government’s total investment in the expressway to
around $2 billion. Just like for other regions, such as Northland, there is no question that
the Government is fully committed to supporting the Waikato and ensuring that it
realises its economic growth potential.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What benefits will the Waikato Expressway deliver?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Many benefits. At least 1,000 jobs will be created once the
final three stages of the expressway get under way. The expressway is a vital piece of
infrastructure, which, once completed, will become the key strategic route for the
Waikato region. It wil l connect the agricultural, tourism, and business centres in the
wider Waikato and Bay of Plenty areas with Auckland. This improved connection will
increase capacity while reducing travel times, reducing fuel and vehicle operating costs,
and reducing the number and severity of accidents in the region.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What reports has the Minister seen on the announcement this week
that work on the final three sections of the Waikato Expressway is set to get under way?

items.speaker: Hon SI MON BRIDGES
items.text: I have seen a report from the chair of the Waikato
Regional Transport Committee, who says: “This is fantastic news and the work will
give a further shot in the arm to the regional economy, road safety and quicker journeys
for both business and the public.” I have also seen a quote from the Mayor of Hamilton,
Julie Hardaker, saying: “This project is a major contributor to economic prosperity, not
only for our region but for New Zealand. Easy, safer, and quicker travel times between
Auckland and Hamilton will provide another boost to Hamilton’s liveability and
economy. We have already experienced the benefits of this roading project with the
sections completed to date.” It is clear from these comments that the Government is
really delivering for t he people of Waikato. Indeed, we are doing so throughout the
regions of New Zealand.
Climate Change Issues, Minister—Performance
7. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co -Leader—Green) to the Minister for Climate

items.speaker: Change Issues
items.text: Is the Government’s objective to increase New Zealand’s net
greenhouse gas emissions or is the Government’s objective to decrease New Zealand’s
net greenhouse gas emissions?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: Decrease.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: In light of that reassuring answer that the objective is to
decrease, does he think he has been a successful climate change Minister given that
New Zealand’s net greenhouse gas emissions have increased by 20 percent since this
Government was elected in 2008?
12 Mar 2015 Oral Questions  2209

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: The spectre of the tall -poppy syndrome hangs menacingly
above my head. I will leave it to others to make a judgment on that.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he think he has been a successful climate change Minister
given that, according to United Nations figures, New Zealand’s carbon intensity has
increased by 14 percent since his Government was elected?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: Leaving the first part of the question aside for the same
reason, let me just say that that figure is completely misunderstood. The reality is that
the Government measures emissions intensity  in terms of percentage of emissions per
unit of real GDP. On that basis—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: The rest of the world is wrong; only Tim Groser is right.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: No, it has been misquoted. On that basis, emissions intensity
in New Zealand has decreased by 30 percent between 1990 and 2012—the exact figure
is 29.2 percent.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to table a report from the Parliamentary L ibrary
showing emissions intensity has increased by 14 percent.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that particular information. Is there any
objection? There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to table a document from the library showing that
New Zealand’s net greenhouse gas emissions have increased 20 percent since 2008.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that p articular information. Is there any
objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he believe he has been successful as a climate change
Minister given that the Ministry for the Environment is projecting a further 48 percent
increase in New Zealand’s net greenhouse gas emissions in the next decade?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: The Government is on tr ack not only to meet its 2008- 12
commitment to reduce net emissions to 1990 levels, but it is absolutely on track to
achieve its objective of reducing emissions further to a minimum of minus 5 percent.
Those are the commitments that we have taken; those are the commitments that we will
meet.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Government on track to meet its publicly announced
target of decreasing emissions by 50 percent by 2050 in light of the Government’s own
projections that show emissions will increase by 50 percent in one decade?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: I am still confident that can be achieved, for a number of
reasons: No. 1, because our forestry cycle will swing sharply back in the other direction
to being a sink for carbon emissions after 2030. Secondly, I think this country has got
every reason to be optimistic that we will find long -term solutions for 70 pe rcent of our
gross emissions in the longer term because approximately 50 percent are agriculture —
48.5 percent is the exact figure. There is major scientific research coming through that is
extremely promising that should be available on the commercial market in 5 to 10 years.
And this country, if you had been listening to the statements Mr Bridges has been
making, is actually ideally placed to make major reductions in transport emissions,
which are 20 percent of New Zealand emissions, as the cost of hybrids  and electric
vehicles continues to reduce given the massive share of renewable electricity in our
country. So if he is—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is a very long answer.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: This graph is relevant to my question, Mr Speaker. Is he proud
of the fact —[Interruption] Yes, that is right; the National Party will cheer, but this
shows New Zealand’s emissions intensity.
2210 Oral Questions  12 Mar 2015

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I know there may be some confusion about what the
particular graph is sho wing, but the member still deserves the opportunity to ask his
question.

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This may help the House. I
do not think you are allowed to table political polls in the House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is not a legitimate point of order. Would the member now get
on with his question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister proud of the fact that the blue line in this graph
is the line of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions  going up by 48 percent —is he
proud of the fact that New Zealand’s emissions are going to go up by 48 percent —and
that the blue line also happens to be the colour of the governing party, and is he
surprised by that?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: Putting  aside exactly what that graph represents and its
authenticity, the answer is that I am very proud to be part of a Government that is going
to deliver on the two international commitments we have to reduce our net emissions.

items.speaker: Dr Russel No rman
items.text: Is it not true that when he is called the Minister for climate
change he really is the Minister for climate change, and a very successful Minister at
that?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: Until the Prime Minister suggests otherwise, I think I do
consider myself the Minister responsible for climate change issues.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This is a wharenui and I
think it is totally inappropriate to have props like that thrown around on the floor of our
House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is a very large prop. The member might have found it easier to
handle if it had been somewhat smaller, but he is allowed a visual aid if it assists—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: It’s on the floor.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do note it fell on the floor —[Interruption] Order! I do not
think that is satisfactory. I was going to allow the member to finish his line of
questioning, and then certainly, if he was not moving to pick it up, I would be asking
him to do so.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given the facts that I have presented showing rapidly increasing
greenhouse emissions, does he want to change his answer to the primary question,
which is that the Government’s objective is actually to increase New Zealand’s net
greenhouse gas emissions and it is doing a jolly good job of it?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will the Minister rise to what he himself has called the great
challenge of our age—climate change— and match the recently announced European
climate target of a 40 percent emissions reduction, or will he continue to keep New
Zealand on track for a 48 percent increase in emissions in the next decade?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: We will meet our existing international contributions, and we
will be consulting the New Zealand public shortly on what should be the next level. In
the process of doing so, we will be pointing out that for a particular set of reasons that
will be clear when members read the discussion document, there is no low-hanging fruit
in New Zealand. If we look at Germany, for example, the 25 percent reduction in gross
emissions was achieved almost exclusively prior to the introduction of the European
emissions trading scheme by closing down lignite c oal stations in eastern Germany.
These soft options do not exist for New Zealand.
Regional Economies—Northland
8. Dr SHANE RETI (National —Whangarei) to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What reports has he received on GDP growth in New Zealand’s regions?
12 Mar 2015 Oral Questions  2211

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yesterday
regional GDP figures for the year ended March 2014 were released by Statistics New
Zealand. They show growth across all New Zealand regions, with a national increase of
6.7 percent. This nominal GDP data, combined with the household labour force survey
data last month showing employment growth of 80,000 jobs in the last year, paints a
strong picture of a broad -based economic recovery. It also highlights the results of the
Government’s continuing focus on economic policies that encourage business
investment in regions right across New Zealand.

items.speaker: Dr Shane Reti
items.text: How is the Northland economy performing compared with the rest
of the economy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Northland’s economy grew at 7.8 percent in the year to
March 2014, which is well above the national average. This—[Interruption] I know that
the Opposition wants to talk that down, but it is the region’s highest annual growth rate
since 2007 and places Northland as one of the top three regions for growth in the North
Island in that year. This strong performance is expected to continue, with the recent
ANZ Regional Trends report highlighting that Northland had recorded the strongest
annual rate of economic growth in the country in December: up 5.1 percent. Northland
is a region that has struggled historically, but these figures highlight that under this
Government Northland’s fortunes are turning round.

items.speaker: Dr Shane Reti
items.text: What other reports has he received on growth in Northland?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The regional GDP figur es continue a strong run of
economic indicators for Northland, with figures out this week also showing that the
region’s tourism sector is having a good run.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: People who live there are wrong! They don’t know what’s going on!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Shh! Too noisy. Northland’s guest nights grew 5.3 percent.
[Interruption] For the member, Northland’s guest nights grew 5.3 percent in the year to
January, and the annual growth in guest nights is now running at 8.1 percent, against the
New Zealand - wide growth rate of 5.6 percent. When you add that to the—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: That’s the March figures. What about before that?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Shh! When you add that to the 7,500 extra new jobs created
in Northland in the last year, it is clear that the region has turned the corner and is
beginning to grow well. To put that employment growth into perspective, the entire
country grew 80,000 jobs last year. So Northland generated, on its own, near ly 10
percent of the country’s job growth.
Partnership Schools—Te Kura Hourua ki Whangaruru Contractual
Arrangements
9. CHRIS HIPKINS (Labour —Rimutaka) to the Minister of Education : Does
she stand by her statement that in the event a charter school closes before the end of its
contract “we will use the usual commercial instruments available to us to recover costs
invested by the Government”; if so, which specific provisions of the contract with
Whangaruru School allow for the recovery of funds in the event the school closes?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yes, to the first part of the
question; in respect of the second part, it would be inappropriate for me to predetermine
the outcome of the process that the school in Whangaruru is currently in.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I was not speculating that the
school was about to close, and it is a question on notice. It is not unreasonable to ask
that the Minister actually give a fulsome answer to a question that has been lodged on
notice.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think that the way forward is I will allow the member an
additional supplementary question.
2212 Oral Questions  12 Mar 2015

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Who owns the 100 hectares of farmland that have been purchased
for Whangaruru School, and which provisions, if any, of the contract with that school
allow for the Crown to make any claim to that land in the event that the school closes?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: The sponsoring trust owns the assets of the school. If I
were to predetermine the outcome of that, I would be anticipating the kind of legal
action we might need to take in the hypothetical situation that that particular school
might arrive at a particular end to the process it is currently in.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Do charter school contracts allow the Government to reclaim any of
the set-up costs or unspent operating costs  in the event that any charter school closes
before its contract has been completed; if so, which clauses in the standard contract
allow for that?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Hon Hekia Parata—either of those two supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Helpfully, the contract is online and has been publicly
available for some considerable period of time, so I could direct the member to it. It
would depend on the nature of the breach of the termination, were it to occur, as to the
remedies available.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Do charter school contracts allow the Government to recoup any
assets at the end of the contract if it is not renewed?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: We have no contracts with charter schools. We have
contracts with partnership schools.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Well, I want to answer truthfully. So, no, I do not have any
charter school contracts.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This is a question on notice. The
words “charter school” are used in the primary question. The words “charter school” are
used in the Government’s confidence and supply agreement with the  ACT Party, which
resulted in these schools being established. If the Minister had a problem with the
terminology, there was plenty of opportunity for her to address that prior to now. To
simply not answer a question, based on the fact that she does not li ke the terminology
that is being used, is unacceptable. It is an offence to the House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, I—

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will allow the Minister to respond.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: The legislation that was passed establishing these legal
entities called partnership schools, and that member was a member of the select
committee, makes it clear at law that what exists is a partnership school. Because the
member is now verging into technicalities relating to the contract, I have said I do not
have a contract with a charter school.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I do not  need further assistance. The difficulty I have with the
Minister’s argument is that when I look at the primary question, which has been
accepted as a question on notice, it does utilise the words “charter schools”. It probably
should not have at the time. It has been there now. I am going to invite the member to
ask that question again.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Do partnership school contracts allow the Government to recoup any
assets, in the event that a contract is not renewed?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: As I have said already, the contract provides for remedies
dependent on the breach, were a school’s contract to be terminated. So I cannot
anticipate which path we might go down, in the hypothetical situation of a school
having its contract terminated.
12 Mar 2015 Oral Questions  2213

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I think the Minister might have
misheard the end part of the question. I was not asking about termination; I was asking
about a contract not being renewed. Those two things are actually quite separate.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think on this occasion the Minister adequately addressed the
question that was asked.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Do partnership school contracts allow the school operators to claim
additional “committed costs” from the Government, in the event of early termination of
their contracts; if so, what is the nature of those conditions?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Hekia Parata—either of those two questions.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I am going to have to ask the member to repeat his question
because I am not clear which particular—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is easy for me to manage. Would the member please
repeat the question, and hopefully it is just one question.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Do partnership school contracts allow the school operators to claim
additional “committed costs” from the Government, in the event of early termination of
their contracts?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I would have to take advice on that because I do not want
to mislead the House, and that is a particular technical question in the contracts. I am
happy to come back.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Didn’t she sign the contracts?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I am not a lawyer.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: How many students are currently on the roll at Whangaruru School
and how many students is it being funded for?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I am advised that there are 37 on the roll and it is being
funded for 40.
Children’s Action Plan—Guidelines for Employers and Statistics
10. Dr PARMJEET PARMAR (National)  to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What recent announcements has she made on steps to protect children?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: On Tuesday I launched
two new guidelines for people and organisations who are working with children, as part
of the Government’s Children’s Action Plan. These guidelines are the first step to help
organisations meet their obligations under the Vulnerable Children Act 2014. The
guidelines Safer Recruitment, Safer Children and Safer Organisations, Safer Children
advise on how employers of the children’s workforce can consistently recruit safe
people to work with children and develop good child protection pol icies. Regulations
are being developed as part of the next step of this process, which will cover the
mandatory requirements that Government agencies must comply with.

items.speaker: Dr Parmjeet Parmar
items.text: How will children benefit from these new guidelines?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The guidelines provide organisations with a standard,
quality, child protection policy to better identify and respond to the needs of vulnerable
children. The recruitment guidelines ensure that people recruited to w ork with children
are assessed in a consistent way. The guidelines give a good cross -sector approach to
good practice and safety checking, from sports clubs to voluntary homework clubs and
cultural groups. Although the vast majority of our children’s worke rs are safe and
conscientious, we do know that predators will seek to work with and be around
children, and we must have robust safeguards in our workforce.

items.speaker: Darroch Ball
items.text: Does the Minister have confidence in the recent Better Public
Services result showing a sharp decline in the number of substantiated cases of child
abuse and neglect?
2214 Oral Questions  12 Mar 2015

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It is true that this year we have seen the first decrease in the
number of substantiated cases of abuse of children, but I w ould say that although we
might celebrate that, it is too early at this stage to be sure that that is a trend.

items.speaker: Darroch Ball
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I asked the Minister quite
specifically whether she had confidence in the recent result, and she did not mention
any confidence or no confidence in that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Does the Minister want to just add to the answer in order to satisfy
the member? I cannot assist.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The latest child abuse statistics show that the number of
children abused in the year ended June 2014 fell by 2,306, or 12 percent, on the
previous year. I would say that the numbers are actually still appallingly high—

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Do you have confidence?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Do I have confidence in the work of Child, Youth and
Family? Yes, of course, but I think what I am saying to you is that it is too soon to know
whether this is a continuing trend. We will have to watch and wait and see and continue
the work we are doing over the next year or so before we can tell whether that decrease
is going to be continued.

items.speaker: Darroch Ball
items.text: How can the Minister be confident now or even in the future in the
Better Public Services results without a public independent audit on how her ministry is
achieving them, or is she going to continue to allow the ministry to act like a self -
licking ice cream and manipulate its own results?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Either of those supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It is very easy to stand in this House and make stupid
comments about some very hard -working public servants who are out there doing their
very best. I have to say that this Government, in introducing a green paper, a white
paper, and a Children’s Action Plan and passing the Vulnerable Children Act, has done
more to protect vulnerable children in this country than that Labour Party  over there did
in Government or than any Government that that member’s party has supported.
Accident Compensation Corporation—Levies and Impact on Government
Financial Position
11. SUE MORONEY (Labour)  to the Minister for ACC : Does she have
confidence in the ACC Board?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Was ACC’s recommendation to reduce levies in the work and earners
accounts ignored by the Government in 2013 and then again in 2015 in order to help the
Government’s books into surplus, as the Prime Minister confirmed in Parliament on
Tuesday when he said it was a factor in that decision?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: The Government has been very consistent in what we have said
about this. We have said that a range of factors are taken into account. Surplus may be
one factor, but also a number of other factors are taken into account. Long -term view in
terms of claimants, our current costs around the scheme, the discount rate —a range of
things are taken into account.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Will she seek an urgent reconsideration of the Government’s levy
rates in light of ACC’s advice to the select committee this morning that its work account
and earners account have already reached the top end of their  funding bands—that is,
the work account has reached 140 percent of what it needs to fully fund the lifetime
costs of accidents and injuries in December—

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: No, that is just not true.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: —that is what the ACC board told the select committee this
morning—while the earners account reached 130 percent of what it requires at the same
time?
12 Mar 2015 Oral Questions  2215

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I think the member needs to listen at the select committee
hearing. What I understand the chair told the select committee today—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: You weren’t there.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: —from National members who were there—was that there has
been a $4 billion shift in January around the overall claims liability. That swung back
by $2 billion in February, but what that demonstrates is the Government’s very fiscally
prudent approach to take a long-term view in terms of ACC.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Is the Minister denying that in December last year the earners account
achieved 140 percent of its funding ratio, and is she denying that the work account
achieved 130 percent of its funding ratio?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: In terms of the work account, I would encourage her to
understand ACC a bit better and to unders tand gradual process, because when you take
into account—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: —gradual process, it is not—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We do have a point of order.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: It was a very specific and direct question—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! There is a lot of noise in the House today. Would the
member please just repeat the question for the Minister to answer.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I cannot read it specifically, but I will relate it. [ Interruption] I will
relate it—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: —because it is not written down. Is the Minister denying that the
work account has achieved 140 percent of its funding ratio as a t December last year and
that the earners account has achieved 130 percent as at December last year?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: With regard to the work account, as I said, she has not taken
into account gradual process —and that is what she continues to fail to do—which
means that the solvency rates come down as a result of that. But the second point that I
would make—and this is the main point here —is that you can take these accounts at a
point in time, but if you do that, you end up in the situation that we had of having a $5
billion deficit in ACC, because you need to take a long- term view because of the
significant shifts in the account. The Labour Party needs to understand that what
businesses need is certainty and stability around levies, not the yo-yo effect of what it is
proposing.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Given that ACC takes into account all of those factors she just
mentioned before it makes recommendations to the Government, will she stop just
making a different excuse every other day about  why she will not return ACC levies to
the right amount and stop overcharging businesses and workers for—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Now the question is going on for too long.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Let me make a couple of points. The first point is, as I have
said before, we need to take a long -term view because otherwise we will end up in the
situation where we have a $5 billion hole. The second point that I would make to the
member is that under our Government we have gone from the $5 bill ion hole to,
essentially, a fully funded scheme. But what businesses do not need is a yo -yo effect,
which is what the Labour Party is promoting. The other point that I would make is that
there has been $1.5 billion worth of reductions under this Government . It is money
back.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Is she aware that section 6 of the Accident Compensation Act, which
she referred to in Parliament on Tuesday, is, in fact, the interpretation section of the Act,
which just tells us what various words mean, and can she explain how that section of the
Act gives her the legal authority to use ACC levies, which are supposed to be gathered
2216 Oral Questions  12 Mar 2015
to pay for injuries and accidents, to achieve a surplus in the Government’s books
instead?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, there are two question there.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Yes, I am aware that section 6 is the interpretation section, but
she needs to read it in the context of both section 330 and section 331(5), and I will read
that out for her—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, no—[ Interruption] Order! That wil l not be necessary.
The Minister was asked the question “Is she aware …”, and she has answered it.
Small Businesses—Growth
12. SCOTT SIMPSON (National —Coromandel) to the Minister for Small

items.speaker: Business
items.text: What steps is this Government taking to support growth for small business?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Small businesses are the
backbone of the New  Zealand economy. This Government has taken a number of steps
through the Business Growth Agenda and the Better Public Services targets to support
growth for small businesses. Another initiative is the regional business partners
programme, which aims to de liver a service valued by small and medium sized
businesses in the regions across New Zealand. In the 6 months to 31 December 2014 the
Regional Business Partner Network has worked with over 1,500 businesses looking to
grow and innovate, providing one-off advice and information, such as raising awareness
of the support available to them, simplifying guidelines and communications, and
improving the consistency of services delivered to small and medium sized enterprises.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: What rep orts has the Minister seen that show that there is growth in
small and medium sized businesses?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I have seen a number of recent reports that confirm there is
growth among small and medium sized businesses. The ANZ Business O utlook report
stated: “Business confidence is buoyant … Businesses remain very optimistic … [and,
as a result] a net 22 per cent expect to be investing more.” The report also talked about
business growth being strongly correlated to GDP growth. New Zealand’s GDP growth
of 3.2 percent and strong GDP growth in the regions of New Zealand will give small
and medium sized businesses even more confidence to grow under the policies and
economic management of this Government.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: What factors would stifle the growth of small business?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: There are a number of factors that would remove flexibility and
stifle the growth of small businesses. They include adding complex new taxes, which
would stifle the growth of small businesses; enforcing and making compulsory
unionised workplaces, which would stifle the growth of small businesses; and reducing
the ability of small businesses to employ people for trial periods would stifle their

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I move, That the New Zealand
Flag Referendums Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Justice and Electoral
Committee to consider the bill. At the appropriate time, I intend to move that the bill be
reported back to the House by 29 July 2015. The Government has made a commitment
to hold a binding referendum on the  New Zealand flag well before the 2017 general
election. As the Prime Minister said last year, it is now an appropriate time for the
debate about the New Zealand flag to be resolved through a careful and considered
process, the main feature of which is to enable New Zealanders to make the decision.
Legislation is required to create a binding referendum process. The Government has
taken a non- partisan approach to this legislation and to the flag consideration process.
2218 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
This bill has been shaped by a cross -party group of MPs, working with initial proposals
set forward by Cabinet. The bill sets out the structure, the procedures, and the
requirements for the referendums; and the requirements for voters, advertisers, and the
Electoral Commission, because it is a u nique process. The referendum process will
uphold the decision of New Zealanders, whether they vote for a new flag, ultimately, or
vote to keep the flag that we have. If a majority of voters choose a new flag, the bill
provides for this to become the offic ial flag of New Zealand by amending the Flags,
Emblems, and Names Protection Act 1981. So it puts those provisions in place, which
does not drive any particular outcome but anticipates a change in the flag.
The Government carefully considered the options around the referendum process and
decided on a two- stage postal process. This begins with a vote on alternative flag
designs and concludes with a clear choice between the current New Zealand flag and the
most preferred alternative design. The first referend um is needed to choose which
alternative flag is most preferred by New Zealanders, including by those who may
ultimately vote against change. The two -stage process means that when voters choose
whether to change our flag, they know what the alternative is. The dates of the
referendums will be confirmed by Order in Council, which offers some flexibility. The
first referendum, though, is currently planned for November/December this year and the
second referendum planned for March 2016—and this timetable has b een discussed by
the cross-party group.
The decision about the voting systems was also made, essentially, by the cross -party
group. They disagreed with the original proposal put forward by Cabinet, and Cabinet
went with the cross -party group’s view. The fi rst referendum will use preferential
voting and will ask New Zealanders to rank four alternative flag designs. They will be
free to rank as many or as few flags as they wish. Preferential voting helps ensure that
the alternative flag goes through with a ma jority support of voters’ preferences. This
system means that all voters can help choose the most preferred alternative flag, so that
the second referendum is really between a representative view and the current flag.
Regardless of how a voter ranks designs in the first referendum, they will be able to
make a clear choice between the current flag and a new flag in the second referendum. I
am sure some people who are strongly motivated will vote for the worst -looking flag in
the first referendum to make sure  that it loses in the second one. Those options are
freely available to every New Zealander.
On this point, I have seen in a media report that Labour Party members may not
support the bill because they think that at the time of the first referendum people should
say whether or not they want change. This issue has been canvassed, and the view set
out in this bill is that a basic tenet of voting is that you need to know what you are
voting for or against. No one is going to know at the time of the first refer endum what
an alternative New Zealand flag will look like. They will know that it could be any one
of four options, but that is quite different from having a simple alternative to the current
flag. So the bill proposes referendums that are the right way ar ound—first, voters
choose an alternative flag design from the four that are on offer, and then they choose
between the alternative and the current flag. The plan that says whether or not you want
the current flag without knowing what the alternative is just does not seem feasible. You
would be voting blind for or against a change to the current flag. I have to say that for
myself, like many New Zealanders, I am kind of biased in favour of the current flag
because I know it, but I am keen to see the alternat ive in order to decide whether to vote
for change. So the voting paper and the wording of the questions are set out in this bill.
The four alternative flag designs for the first referendum will be determined through
consultation with the public. I must str ess that that consultation will be organised and
led by an independent panel. The Flag Consideration Panel will recommend flag
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2219
designs to me as the responsible Minister, and Cabinet will confirm the four options to
be added to the first referendum voting paper by Order in Council. I think the
independence of that process is absolutely vital. I have worked with the chair of the
Flag Consideration Panel in the past, and I am sure that the professor will make sure it
remains independent, because the process he re is as important as the result. The Flag
Consideration Panel’s consultation and how it will choose the shortlist of designs is not
part of this bill. It is not a matter for Parliament and it is not a matter for Cabinet; it is a
matter for the panel. The submission of flag designs to the panel will be separate from
the select committee stage for this bill. The bill simply provides that the designs
recommended by the panel and confirmed by Cabinet are inserted into the voting paper
by Order in Council. The select committee stage will give the public the opportunity to
make submissions about the referendum  process itself, not about flag designs, although
I am sure that will become part of the discussion.
The Electoral Commission will discuss these referendums , and it has robust systems
in place. A District Court judge will observe the secure processing and counting of the
votes. The votes will be processed centrally as they are returned over a 3- week postal
voting period. The order of the flags on the voting paper will be determined randomly.
All eligible voters on the electoral roll will be able to vote. As with elections, voters
who are overseas will also be able to participate.
The bill also sets out rules for the regulation of  referendum advertising. The
Government, on the recommendation of the cross -party group, has decided that this
regulation should not be heavy -handed. An advertiser will not be subject to rules or
limits on its spending. The only requirement will be that promotional advertisements
contain a promoter statement. This requirement will not apply to the display of the
current New Zealand flag or alternative designs that are on the voting paper unless they
are accompanied by further promotional material about voting in the referendums.
People should be free to display the flag of their country unencumbered. This will allow
for wide public discussion on the flag without unnecessarily restricting freedom of
expression. If voters choose to change the flag, this will trigger provisions in the bill t o
change to the new flag within 6 months. It is important that people do not see these
provisions in the bill as predetermining the outcome of the referendum; they simply put
in place the mechanism needed if the flag changes. If it does not, those mechanisms will
not be required. The only legal requirements for the use of the official flag relate to
drivers’ licences and New Zealand - registered ships. If the flag changes, there will be a
further 6-month transitional period.
I am grateful for the input of members from other parties who participated in the
development of this bill, which will give New Zealanders a chance to have their say on
a vital symbol of nationhood. I suspect that once the Cricket World Cup passes, which
has excited strong feelings of p atriotism, and hopefully more, this will become a matter
of some wide public interest. I welcome the public debate and consideration as this bill
passes through the select committee. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I agree with quite a lot of
what the Deputy Prime Minister has said in his introductory speech on the bill. I think
he has summarised the issues relatively well, save for one or t wo. According to the
latest published poll done by Television New Zealand, 65 percent of voters are opposed
to changing the flag, and 2 percent of New Zealanders think that it is an important issue.
Labour believes, as was the case with the MMP referenda s eries, that New Zealanders
should have the right to say no as part of the first referendum, rather than having to wait
until the second. We think that if there is a clear view early on that New Zealanders do
not want to proceed with a change in the flag, t hen we should not spend the tens of
millions of dollars that will be involved in conducting a second referendum. I might say
2220 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
that the Labour Party was not alone at the select committee with that point of view. At
the final meeting of the committee there wa s only one party—and that was the National
Party—opposed to New Zealanders having the right to say no as part of the first
referendum. So let us make it clear that every other party that was represented and
present at what was meant to be a multi -party, co nsensus-building - committee is
opposed to or has indicated they were opposed to the approach that Mr English is taking
with this referendum. I think that also, for me, shows a bit of the problem.
This has clearly become what might be described as a “vanit y project” for the Prime
Minister. It is something that he strongly believes in. I actually think we should change
our flag. I am of the view that it is time to change the flag, but what is really important
is that we get the process right. I just totally reject —totally reject—the suggestion by
the Deputy Prime Minister that New Zealanders are not bright enough to understand
that they have a yes/no vote twice. It was maybe 20 years ago that we went through a
similar process to change our electoral system, w here we had a yes/no vote and a run-
off of choices as part of the first ballot, and the second ballot was the then current
system versus the new system. People could understand that. People are not thick. But it
left them with the choice to say no at the beginning. And in this particular case, it would
save tens of millions of dollars. Frankly, anyone who spends a bit of time in a
constituency, who talks to parents with special needs kids, who looks into schools and
their operational funding, and who looks at the poverty in New Zealand knows that
there are many better uses for the tens of millions of dollars that are going to be spent,
including on the second part of the process, than a flag referendum. But as we know,
this is a vanity project for the Prime Minister.
I must say that Jonathan Young is looking fitter as a result of this process. I do not
think I have ever seen anyone run up and down the Beehive stairs as much as Jonathan
Young did in consulting with the Deputy Prime Minister on this particular issue.
Frankly, I have been involved in a couple of multi -party committees of this sort in the
past, and I have never seen one where the Government pulled the strings of the chair in
such a way. I like Mr Young. I think he is a good character. He actually comes from a
damn solid family, but in this particular case he did not understand the role of the chair
in defending the views of the other parties to the executive, and he allowed himself to
be dictated to by them.
The Flag Consideration Panel itself, I t hink it is fair to say, is a mixture. It is a
mixture of some wonderful people and a few National Party hacks. It is sad—it is really
sad—that the executive, that Cabinet, was not prepared to accept the list that was
prepared by the multi-party committee, which had plenty of extra choices.

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: Most of them are.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: No, eight out of the 12 are, and four out of the eight —
four out of the eight —are people whom Jonathan Young nominated. So, act ually, a
third of the people who are on that panel are people who were nominated by other
parties. So just do not interrupt and do not interject, Bill English, when you do not know
what you are talking about. When you do not know what you are talking about , Bill
English, it pays to keep those slightly split lips together. It pays to keep those slightly
split lips together, Mr English.
There were some other revealing things at the committee. I learnt, as part of the
committee, a lot about the ACT Party and its attitude to primary industry in New
Zealand. It is a quote that will stay with me for ever —the quote from David Seymour,
the leader of the ACT Party. He indicated that farmers are not business people. We had
a couple of nominations there for farmers to be on the panel, and Mr Seymour said:
“Unless they invented dairy farming, they’re not real business people.” That is an
Epsom indication of the value of agriculture to New Zealand if ever I saw it. At the
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2221
moment what is happening is that the National Party is relying on a person with that sort
of attitude towards primary production for its majority.
Another point goes to timing. I will accept that there are times when a committee
accepts your point of view and there are times when it does not. This is one  time when
the committee clearly did not accept my point of view. I think that having the second
referendum—and I think possibly we should not —in the lead-up to the centenary of the
first commemoration of Gallipoli lacks taste. I think it lacks taste. I th ink having a 3-
week period less than a month before the centenary of the first commemoration of
Gallipoli is something where our soldiers —we had only had the flag for 13 years at the
time of Gallipoli, but I think there is a certain lack of sensitivity and a denigrating of the
role of the military. I am an old Viet Nam protester, but I think some of the attitudes of
members from that side of the House towards people who have served New Zealand
leave something to be desired. The timing insisted on by the Dep uty Prime Minister for
this is part of that.
So it is with a slightly heavy heart—because I do want to change our flag —that I am
indicating that Labour will not support this bill until New Zealanders get the right to say
no as a part of the first referendum.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Well, if all Labour members can come up
with as a reason not to support this bill is that they do not like the way the questions are
asked, then it seems like a pretty flimsy reason to me. I mean, really, is that it? Is that
the strength of the argument that Labour members could promote —that, actually, they
do not like the order of the questions?
Here is how I think about it. If I am going to make a decision about whether or not
New Zealand is going to have a change of flag, I would like to think that I would be
given some context about what I might potentially be voting for or not. And, in the first
referendum, I can withhold that choice, and that gives me quite a bit of power, actually.
I do not know whether the Assistant Speaker has actually thought it t hrough very much,
to be frank. If I felt really passionately about it, I could design a flag myself. How
powerful is that? So that is three goes that I have got over this.
In the first instance, if I felt really, really strongly about replicating that little hand -
embroidered kiwi that my mum had on her knapsack when she went hitchhiking around
the UK 50 years ago —and she felt so proud to be a Kiwi, to be a New Zealander —if I
felt so proud of that, which I do, then I could promote that as my idea for the fla g. The
commission that will be enacted under this bill will be able to evaluate that against all of
the other suggestions that come through from fellow New Zealanders. It might be a kiwi
like the one on my mum’s knapsack, or it might be a silver fern, or i t might be that
wonderful—wonderful—image of a silver fern with the servicemen marching off into
the distance: a really poignant symbol for many people of what it means to be a New
Zealander, and it has been translated into a tattoo and has gone viral around the world.
People feel really strongly about this kind of thing.
How come I am standing up here in this Parliament, for example, remembering that
my mum had an embroidered kiwi on her knapsack 50 years ago when she went off on
her big adventure? Why? Be cause it meant a lot to her and it means a lot to me. So the
flag is a really important aspect of us, as New Zealanders, defining who we think we
are. What is it in our flag that defines who we are? Not only is it when we are
remembering the wonderful things that New Zealanders have done for us and by us and
to us—not just that —but it is also our outward- facing nature, which we do so well in
this country. It is our face to the world, and to a lot of people it means a lot. So strike
one for me is that I have  the opportunity, which is described in this bill, to design my
own flag, based on what is important to me, and to submit it to be part of the
consideration.
2222 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
Strike two is the first referendum question. That first referendum question is going to
say: “Here are four alternatives. Which one do you like, New Zealand?”. We know we
have got the old one, and here it is in the bill. It is the third flag we have had in our
history, by the way. So there we are; we have got that one in the bag. We have had it
since 1902. It has served us well. We are proud of it. But does it say who we are today?
OK, so we have that. The question for me and for every other New Zealander —except
the Labour Party members because, of course, they do not want to have a question; they
are going to oppose it. Except the Labour Party members because they do not like the
way the questions are framed, so they are not even going to play with us. Oh, well,
