that’s fine. But, I, as a New Zealander, am going to. And when I have my second
strike—my second choice—I am going to be able to vote, and it is going to be a vote
based on four flags that mean a lot to New Zealanders. Well, what a wonderful
opportunity that is. I am looking forward to that very much.
As I read the bill very briefly this afternoon, I think that that vote is going to happen
around May 2016. So that is quite a tight time frame. If you have got a mind to start
designing the flag, I would get on to it this afternoon. I have got some blank paper; I
might do it after this speech. That is my second strike, and that is an exciting prospect
for all of us because we all have the opportunity to make a choice. If we did not have
our flag, which we have here in the bill —if we did not have this one, which one would
we like? Which one most captur es what it means to me to be a New Zealander? What a
powerful question. Why does Labour not support that? Why does Labour not support
the absolute power and freedom of a New Zealander to be able to answer a question like
that? Well, it beats me. [ Interruption] Oh, OK, my colleague from Rangitīkei has just
said: “Well, because it wasn’t their idea.” OK, I leave it at that.
In around May next year an envelope will arrive in the mail for all of us who are
registered electors, and we will get the opportunity to choose between four options. At
that point, what that allows us to do, apart from choosing something that speaks to us
about being a New Zealander, is to begin to weigh up in our minds: OK, if we are not
going to have the current flag, what might we repla ce it with? Is that not a much better
question than a simple yes or no? We will have something in front of us that we can
look at—we will be able to see those designs. They will be in the newspaper. They will
be in the media. They will be in social media, no doubt. They will be on the voting
papers. Is that not a more powerful position for us as New Zealanders to be able to say:
“OK. Is it the old one or might it be one of these? I’m going to think about that and then
I am going to have a vote.”? And, for m e, I do not know yet. I do not know; I am open.
But I am looking forward to those alternatives, which I might vote on. So that is strike
two.
Then, as enacted under this bill, the commission goes away and determines a
preference, and then, and only then, puts that preference— and it might well be a silver
fern on a red and blue background. It might well be a kiwi. It could be anything. It could
be the Southern Cross. It could be a combination of the old flag and some aspect of
New Zealand that speaks to us n ow. We do not know what it is going to be, and that is
what is so wonderful about this process. In due course —third strike—we are going to
have another choice, and that choice is going to be based on a bit of thinking. Unlike
Sue Moroney, who is sitting over on the other side of the House just yabbering away,
because I do not think she understands the issue —because what we are going to be able
to do—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: I think it’s Jacqui Dean who’s yabbering.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Well, that got them going. What we are going to be able to do, in
another 6 or so months’ time, is make a decision based on knowledge —make a decision
based on some options about what really speaks to us, as New Zealanders. Well, how
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2223
wonderful is that? What an opportunity for us, as New Zealanders. So when we do go to
make that final vote, in about a year and a half’s time, we will be able to make a
decision based on knowledge. And that is what the Labour Party is voting against. It
does not want us to go to thi s referendum being able to make a decision based on
knowledge. It has just knee -jerked: “We’ve got to oppose it, we’ve got to oppose it,
we’ve got to oppose it. What could we oppose it on? I know: they’ve got the questions
around the wrong way.” Well, if that is the best that Labour members can come up with,
then maybe they deserve to be floundering around the 33 percent in the —what, 33, 32
percent? Are they in the 30s? Whatever.
This bill puts a structure in place for New Zealanders to have a say about our  flag—
and it is our flag, and it is not just going to be the Labour Party telling us how to vote.
This is going to be a binding referendum for all New Zealanders. It is a marvellous
opportunity, and I support this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: There is a fundamental flaw in what
Jacqui Dean was saying, and I would just invite Mrs Dean to think back to the last time
we had a binding referendum. It was in 2011 and it was on MMP —nothing more
fundamental than our voting system. Was the first referendum —and there could have
been two—on whether we wanted single transferable vote, supplementary member, first
past the post, or MMP, and when we decided what the alternative was we  would decide
whether we kept the status quo? Of course not. The last time we had a binding
referendum in this country, the electorate of New Zealand was quite properly asked,
first of all: “Do you want to change the voting system?”. That is why the whole logic of
the referendum on a flag, if we are going to have the referendum, is: let New Zealanders
decide first of all whether we want to change the flag. Why would we spend $26 million
on two referendums if the majority of New Zealanders did not want change?
I have got the three latest polls on the flag, and I have got to say that the Television
New Zealand (TVNZ) one on September 2014 was 35 percent for change, 65 percent
against. The March 2014 New Zealand Herald poll was 40 percent for change and 52
percent against. The February 2014 TVNZ poll was 28 percent for change, 72 percent
against. So here we have got a Government that wants to have change —and I will come
to what my view is on that shortly —but it is going  to say what we are going to change
to before it gives New Zealanders the right to say whether or not they want it. This is
not a decision for 121 members of Parliament to make in this Chamber; this is a
decision for all New Zealanders. Surely we should as k New Zealanders the first
question in the logical order: “Do you want change?”. Is there anything that is not
understandable about that priority? That is how we decided on our voting system. That
is how we could be deciding on our flag.
The other thing a bout those polls that I have just talked about is that the TVNZ poll
found the total of all of the New Zealanders who thought that changing the flag was an
important issue. Do you know what the total came to? Two percent —2 percent of New
Zealanders thought that this was an important issue. It is, therefore, hard to understand
what the obsession of the Prime Minister is with this issue. On the one hand it could be
a vanity project. The Prime Minister is about to retire and he wants to be remembered
for something. It is hard to think what he will be remembered for, but maybe he could
be remembered for changing the flag. The alternative explanation for why the Prime
Minister has this obsession is that it is a bit like bread and circuses. It is a great
diversion, is it not? When things are not happening the way they should be around the
country, let them look at something else: “Watch this flag. See we could change this
flag. Don’t worry about education. Don’t worry about the failure of the charter schools
and the loss of public money. Don’t worry about the district health boards not having
enough to provide decent health services. Don’t worry about the fact that we have cut
2224 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
policing in real terms every year in the last 5 years. Look at the flag.” That is a
diversion.
You know, I probably share with most New Zealanders the kind of bemusement
about why this is being put up as a priority issue. I noticed that the American comedian
John Oliver also said that. He said that the New Zealand Prime Minister —to his
audience, if they knew where New Zealand is —was going to change the flag. Then he
went on and said that John Key, as the newly elected Prime Minister, is “ready to tackle
the most pressing issues facing the country.” Well, I disagree —I disagree. John Oliver
was obviously being sarcastic about that.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: No!

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Just for the dimmer members across the House, I thought I
should explain that in case Government members got excited.
I think there are other priorities. I think the  level of child poverty in our country is a
priority. Why would we not be focusing on that in a debate this afternoon? I think the
transport gridlock in Auckland is a priority. They have to worry about that—

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: No, not to the National Party—not to the National Party.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Well, maybe not in the Wairarapa, Mr Mark, but certainly for a
third of the country who are Aucklanders. I think the housing crisis where every year
fewer and fewer New Zealanders get the chance to own their own home is a priority. So
I do not know why we have a priority where we are going to be spending $26 million on
a couple of referendums in the wrong order —a couple of referendums in the wrong
order. I know that the people in Mt Roskill will be asking me when I go back there
tonight: “Why are we spending $26 million? Is there nothing better that the National
Government has got to spend it on?”. I could say that it is spending $65 million on
sending 16 trainers to Iraq—that is not too good—and it is spending $69 million on
trying to buy an election, which is being totally counter -productive. So I guess my
confession to my electorate will be that the Government is wasting lot of money, and
this $26 million is part of the wastage.
There are a couple of other things that I think we need to take into account. If we are
trying to cut down the cost of it, it makes sense to have one referendum first to see
whether people want to have change. But there is another proposal that I have for the
House, and that is that if we are going to have a referendum on something as significant
as the symbol of the country, the flag, why would we not hold that at the same time as
an election? There are two big advantages in that. The first, of course, is that it is much
cheaper, but the second advantage is that you are going to get a decent turnout. If you
have a stand -alone referendum, you might get 40 percent, or maybe 50 percent, going
out to vote. I am saying that if you are going to change the flag, at least get a genuine
indicator of what people feel, and the best way to do that is by coinciding a referendum
with an election. Is it so pressing that we have to have two stand- alone referendums
before the next election? Nobody thinks it is that pressing. Two percent of New
Zealanders think that changing the flag is an important issue. So let us be logical.
Let us in this House be sensible, and I am directing this to the members of the
National caucus. Why not have at the next election one referendum with two parts? Part

items.speaker: A will ask
items.text: “Do you want to change the flag? Yes or no?”. Easy. Then Part B will ask:
“If there is a majority that wants to change the flag, which of these preferences do you
prefer?”. You do not have to run it as two separate stand- alone referenda. You coul d
hold it with one referendum coinciding with the election. What is illogical about that? It
is totally sensible. It is what we should be doing. That is what every party on the cross -
party committee wants to do, with the exception of National and, if you c all it a stand -
alone party, ACT. That is what the majority of people in this House want.
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2225
My own preference is that I would actually like to see a new flag —a 21 st century
flag—and I kind of like the one by Kyle Lockwood. It has the silver fern through the
middle. It has the blue of the Pacific, and the Southern Cross, and it is three colours. It
is quite attractive. But it is not my decision to make.
There is something else I want to say about timing. When the RSA makes as strong a
stand as it has, I think we should do it the courtesy of listening to it. We all say: “What a
debt we owe to our veterans.”, and, by God, we do owe a debt to our veterans. So why
would you, as the Prime Minister, introduce a bill to change the flag a month before the
centenary of Anzac Day—a month before the most important day for our veterans, and,
because it is the centenary, the most important one in 100 years?

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: That’s pathetic.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: This is just throwing it up into their faces, Mr Smith. That is
what it is doing. Why could we not have waited for the RSA and our veterans? They
feel strongly about it and I understand why they feel strongly about it. They fought
under that flag, Dr Smith, something you and I have neve r had to do. They saw their
mates die under that flag. They feel strongly about it. I have a different view on the flag
but I do respect their view, and I do respect the fact that in a month’s time we will be
commemorating the centenary of the Anzacs. I th ink we could do them at least the
courtesy of waiting until after that before we start this debate and bring this legislation
into the House. I have to say that the logic is entirely in favour of having one
referendum with the first question asking whether  people want to change the flag and
the second part asking what they want to change it to. We should do it at the same time
as the general election, to save the $26 million the Government is spending and to get a
decent turnout in terms of the answers to both those questions.
I have to say, as well, because it has been raised time and again with me, that there is
a panel of 12 people. Some of them are very good people. Some of them are National
Party hacks. We could have cut that committee down. In my elec torate, where people
are struggling to pay their rent and make sure their kids get what they want, people are
wondering why there is $600 to $800 a day being paid to National Party hacks to sit on
the panel. That is wrong, and I am against that as well.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I would like to point out to the House, before I call on
the next speaker, that the debate is relatively narrow. It is around process, around
timing, and the previous speakers have covered that quite wel l. It is not an argument
about what other things taxpayers’ funds could be expended on. It is not a wide -ranging
debate. It is narrow, and, as we have heard from previous speakers, there is plenty to
talk about around the process, the timing, and the other provisions within the bill.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: This is a very great opportunity to be able to come
and talk about something that is of such significance to New Zealand, to our nation, that
we need to spend some significant time talking about it. We need to ensure we have a
good process, so that we make a good decision at the end of the process.
This is a very important debate. It is not something you would do once every
parliamentary term. It is not something you would do every 10, 20, 30, or even 40 years.
But it is something that should, or perhaps could, be done every 100 years or so. The
current flag was put in place in 1902, so it probably is a good time for us to stop and
ponder the future of  our flag in New Zealand. The last 100 years have seen some
significant changes in our country, good changes a lot of them; different changes at
different times. But if a flag is to be a unifying symbol of sovereignty, of our heritage
and our values, then from time to time, albeit every 100 years or so, perhaps it is
appropriate for us to have another look at it and ask whether the flag still reflects our
heritage, our sovereignty, our values, and the make-up of our nation.
2226 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
It is an important debate but it is also an emotional debate. As has been said by many
speakers, this flag is one that has been fought under. It is one that people have died
under. It is a flag that has been draped over the shoulders of gold medallists and has
been raised while our anthe m has been played on many different occasions. It is a flag
that has been flown at half mast on sombre occasions. A lot of emotion is attached to
those different events when the flag is involved. So we need to be careful in our
process, how we go about it, and how we address any potential change to it.
It is also a potentially divisive debate. We have already seen from what has been said
in the House this afternoon that there are differing views even on the process, and also
differing views on what the fla g of New Zealand should look like. If I may coin a
phrase from the Australian State of Origin series, it is the kind of issue that would pit
mate against mate. It is the kind of thing that there will be much debate over, at the
barbecues, in the pubs, and in the school classrooms. Because it is a divisive debate, it is
something we need to handle with care. It is something we should not necessarily lump
in with a general election; it is something that is deserving of having that singular focus
in terms of the way we address this issue.
Before really thinking about this, I asked myself a number of questions. They were
questions I asked myself, but they were also questions other people have asked while I
have been speaking to them as I have gone out and about  on my business. The first
question is why we are having this debate. Is it really worth the emotional trauma that
seems to be going along with it? Is it really worth the potential divisiveness? The
answer is yes, because there has been a growing level of interest across our nation in
debating this issue and in people having their say about whether we should retain the
flag we have or change it.
So it is worth it. It is something that reflects, I think, our society as it is, where
people are questioning al l sorts of things, from whether or not we should keep the
monarchy—I do not want to get side -tracked into that debate today. While those
questions are resounding around our communities, it is absolutely worth us having this
debate and this discussion. What ever the outcome of this process, whether it be that we
keep the existing flag or we change the flag, we will be better for it, I believe, as a
nation, because we will have really wrestled with the issues that surround our national
heritage, our national values, and how we reflect that through a flag.
So I asked myself the question why people are looking at this now. Why is it an
important decision for people to be making now? What is so wrong with our current
flag? One of the big things I hear from so man y people is that in one corner of the flag
is the Union Jack, and that reflects only a very small part now of our New Zealand
heritage. I know that for me, my English heritage looks and can find St George’s cross,
and my Scottish heritage looks and can find the St Andrew’s cross. The part of me that
is a bit Irish cannot find anything in there to celebrate. That is probably pretty much
reflected, I think, by anybody with Irish descent when it comes to the Union Jack. But I
think that although we have the Union Jack there, there are some people who would do
it. It reflects only one part of our culture.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: A small part.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: Yes, absolutely a small part. We hear at the moment just how
many people we have from other natio ns, not simply from the United Kingdom. This
New Zealand place is not the United Kingdom. There is, in fact, a plethora of people
from all sorts of cultures. There is nothing on our flag currently that, for example, really
signifies anything of significanc e to do with Māori. I am not here to argue the fors and
againsts of this flag but merely to highlight that a number of people have shown some
issues with the flag, and therefore it is worthy of debate.
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2227
I find it really interesting, actually, that now New Zealand First members want to talk
about it, but when it came to being participants in the cross -party meeting we had about
it, they were nowhere to be seen. They did not want to be part of it then, but now they
want to shout across the House and talk about it. I find that a little bizarre.
[Interruption] Anyway, if I can possibly hear myself over the rant from the other side, I
might be able to carry on with what I really want to say.
The question I then asked myself was whether this is the right process. This is such a
significant process that it needs to be done formally. It needs to be done carefully and,
for all the reasons that have been outlined already in the House today, it needs to be
done respectfully. So we invited all of the parties to be a part of it, and we have come up
with a process that I think is one that is going to really bring out the very best result that
we can achieve. I think that the approach we are taking is the right one. I know there
was some discussion, for example, about the voting system that would be used, and I
am glad to see we are using a preferential system now. I think that that was a very good
part of what came out of the cross -party discussion. I have got a bit of experience with
preferential voting. We had the single transferable vote (STV) in my days as Mayor of
Palmerston North, and it served me pretty well, I have to say; at least on the one
occasion that we had STV when I was running for election. I think it is good because it
ensures that whatever alternative comes up, the fact that more than 50 percent of people
agree is better than any other option that is on the table. I think that that is a very good
process.
I am not normally one in favour of referendums. When we had a lot of talk during
the election about whether we should have binding citizens initiated referenda and the
like, I was not very happy about the idea because so often when you have a binding
referendum of any kind, the question can be very much flawed and lead to a level of
ambiguity. But I think that the questions we have that are related to these two
referendums clearly point us in the right direction to ensure we will get a very positive
result for New Zealand.
I want to address the order of the two questions and the order of the two
referendums, which has been sort of disputed, I guess, by the other side of the House. I
am concerned that people do not want to engage in the debate before they simply write
it off, and that is what is being proposed by having this yes or no choice up front. I for
one have not made up my mind as to whether or not I believe we should change the
flag, quite simply because I do not know what the alternative would be. There are many,
many people I know out there who are yet to make up their minds whether or not they
believe we should change the flag, because they are waiting to see what the alternative
would be. Putting a yes or no choice up front eliminates them from the equation. So we
have got the process right. We are moving in the right direction.
Finally, I just w ant to touch on the point that people have said there are more
important issues right now for us to discuss. If I were to ask whether this is the most
important issue for New Zealand right now, of course the answer would be no. But I
have complete confidence in this Government—while it is still working hard to improve
the educational outcomes of New Zealand, which we are doing; while we are working
hard on delivering Better Public Services, which we are doing; and while we are
continuing to work towards bet ter health targets, which we are achieving —also being
able to cope with this issue. That is something we are seeking to do.
So, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, no doubt it is of no surprise to you, in summary, that
I absolutely support this process. It is a g ood process, it is a healthy process, and it is
one that I believe will deliver whatever result is the right result for New Zealand and for
our flag going forward. Thank you.
2228 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: We have before us the New Zealand Flag
Referendums Bill. In one respect, it can be seen as a matter of considerable political
significance. In another sense, there is less to it than meets the eye. What meets the eye
is the visual symbolism of our national identity. Flags count, at least in the sense of self-
perception. They depict who we think we are, to paraphrase a recently departed
colleague. The Canadians got it right, back in the 1960s. The simple but compelling
symbol of the maple leaf beaut ifully illustrates who the Canadians are. The world
recognises them immediately and positively. Those of us in Australasia are a little
slower in the maturation process. We have lingered with the Union Jack as both the
colonial symbol and our national flag . The other symbol, the Southern Cross, is shared
between our two countries. It simply serves to sow confusion as to our separate
identities, yet Brazil has the Southern Cross as well. So we could retain the stars and
still have a separate identity. There is, therefore, a compelling reason to consider a
change of flag. We would, so to speak, be proceeding down a road of national
significance.
But there is also less to this than meets the eye. The way in which the process has
been generated is a trifle weir d, because it was the Prime Minister who took it upon
himself to lead the nation in the idea of changing the flag. The explanatory note says:
“For some time there has been public debate about whether New Zealand should
consider changing its flag.” That is,  of course, contestable, as a quick review of the
flag’s history will show. We have had the current version since it was first gazetted back
in 1869 and affirmed in 1902. The insertion of the Southern Cross was done on the
instruction of the Queen- in-Council—not exactly a public debate. As early as 1920
Parliament was asked to consider whether to have a flag that was distinct from that of
Britain. Queries were already being received from the Canadian Parliament. New
Zealand MPs replied then that there needed to be “a groundswell of public opinion
before the Government should consider any change.” During World War II suggestions
were made to the Prime Minister that a Māori emblem be included on the flag, in
recognition of the role of the Māori Battalion. Pete r Fraser deferred the matter until the
end of the war, and it was never revisited.
In 2004 a civic movement was formed to change the flag, with a campaign for a
citizens initiated referendum. But there was not enough support to force a vote. To the
extent that there was any public debate, the people pre- emptively voted for no change.
The latest development was in 2009, with the refusal of Transit New Zealand to fly the
Tino Rangatiratanga flag on the Auckland Harbour Bridge. The critical development
that time was the decision by the Prime Minister to personally intervene. He said he
would be happy to allow a Māori flag to be flown, including in Parliament, if there were
agreement over a particular design. A series of hui followed to ascertain which of four
flags Māori preferred. The choice was between the New Zealand flag, the independence
flag, the red ensign, and the Tino Rangatiratanga flag. The last one was chosen, and it
has flown on Waitangi Day ever since. But whether that represents a spontaneous and
genuine public debate about changing our national flag is a separate thing and more than
just a moot point.
The Prime Minister, with his instinct for vice -regal populism, has actually sparked
this latest round himself, with his speech 1 year ago. He said then that he was outlining
“a plan to hold a public discussion and vote, next parliamentary term, on New Zealand’s
flag.” The Prime Minister cannot outline a plan to hold a public discussion about a
change of flag and say, on introducing the bill, that for some time there has been a
public debate. That is the debate he is planning to hold, not one that he can
acknowledge already exists.
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2229

items.speaker: The second point of concern
items.text: in his speech last year the Prime Minister allowed
himself the luxury of stating a personal  belief. “The design of the current flag
symbolises a colonial and post -colonial era whose time has passed.” he told an
unsuspecting nation. He said: “I am proposing that we take one more step in the
evolution of modern New Zealand by acknowledging our independence through a new
flag.” Yet in the next breath the Prime Minister said he wanted to give a clear assurance
and commitment that retaining the current flag was a very possible outcome from the
process, and there was to be no presumption in favour of c hange. The Prime Minister
cannot have it both ways. He cannot gratuitously offer a personal view that the flag
should be changed, and in the same speech say there was no presumption in favour of
change. Of course there is a presumption. It is on the part of the nation’s leader. Had he
kept his personal views to himself, the disclaimer might have come across as genuine.
The conclusion is clear. The Prime Minister is not responding to a public clamour for
change. He is personally stimulating a process for a d ecision, and in that process has
already stated his view.
In fairness, the way his Cabinet has structured the national decision process is
broadly democratic. The explanatory note says: “To provide New Zealanders with a
forum in which to progress this dis cussion in a formal and respectful way, the
Government decided to initiate a broad engagement process, followed by the
opportunity for the public to vote on the New Zealand Flag.” The cross -party group, the
citizens panel, and the dual referenda are that p rocess. But the basic presumption that
there was a strong mandate for a change remains in question. That doubt has not been
allayed; if anything it has been intensified by the refusal of Cabinet to agree to the
recommendation of the cross -party group that the first referendum include a prior
question: “Do you think the flag should be changed?”. If a simple majority were to say
no, there would not be a second referendum. That would have been truly democratic.
That would have implemented the assurance that there was no presumption on his part
for change. But Cabinet refused, so we are obliged to go through the process of the two
referenda.
There are many people out there saying that this process is a distraction or a $26
million waste of public funds when there are more pressing social and political needs. It
would have been consistent with those concerns for the Prime Minister to agree that the
basic question be asked first, but he has presumed to override that. This fact alone
brings into doubt the credibili ty of his claim that there is a public debate already
existing but no presumption of change. In his 2014 speech the Prime Minister claimed
that the decision over the flag is “bigger than party politics”. This is true. That is why he
should have listened with more respect to the recommendation of the cross-party group.
The Green Party will support this bill going to the select committee, but we shall
listen very carefully to the submissions and gauge the public mood. We shall not take
the Prime Minister’s word for it that it is critically important to proceed. The decision to
proceed should and must reflect a genuine national decision, not a personal preference
of a populist leader.

items.speaker: DENIS O'ROURKE
items.text: I am really quite saddened to have to speak on this
bill today, because I, and we in New Zealand First, do not see why it is needed at all. It
is not clear why suddenly this legislation for a new flag has arisen under the leadership
of the Prime  Minister. The motivation is certainly not clear. For many years there has
been sporadic public debate about whether New Zealand should consider changing its
flag, but it has been at a very, very low level and it has nearly always been associated
with the republican movement. So is National really just taking the first step towards
republicanism? Has it become infected with republicanism and is that what it really is
going to do later? Maybe this is just the first step. Or is it a career succession plan for
2230 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
John Key, first President of New Zealand? What really is the motivation for this? It is
certainly not clear to us.
At the very least, this is a way of diverting public attention away from much more
urgent issues. It is a blue herring. We should be looking much more at spending our
energy, our money, and our efforts on issues like child poverty; a rundown health
service in many regions; a 1960s transport system on its last legs; an education system
riddled with inequities and misguided investment; an  undiversified economy far too
dependent on one or two products, dairying and tourism, and one market, China; an out -
of-control immigration system, resulting in excessive net migration—

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: What a load of rubbish.

items.speaker: DENIS O'ROURKE
items.text: —a worsening housing crisis, and the list goes on. If that
member thinks it is a load of rubbish, he should ask the people of New Zealand, because
they think those issues are much more—much more—important than a new flag for this
country. You have only to ask them to find that out. The Government has appointed a
flag consideration panel, which it is paying at a rate of, I understand, somewhere
between $600 and $800 per day, its purpose being “to lead public engagement and to
recommend alternative flag designs for New Zealanders to consider through
referendum”. But this is not just a waste of millions of dollars of public money for no
public benefit. In fact, New Zealanders will not really get to make the decision at all,
because they will have presented to them only four options actually decided by others.
The whole process is being so rushed that it is clear that the Government wants to make
sure this is done before the next election, for some reason—maybe as John Key’s legacy
to New Zealand after he loses that election.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Ha, ha! In your dreams, pal.

items.speaker: DENIS O'ROURKE
items.text: And we will soon see—and we will soon see. The first step of
that will be when the Government loses the Northland by -election in a few days’ time.
The bill establishes a process for the holding of two postal referendums, the first to
determine which alternative flag design is preferred from only four alternatives, and the
second to determine whether that alternative or the current flag should be the New
Zealand flag. That is the final part of the referendum. So there are two referendums,
effectively. If the voters decide in the second referendum that the flag is to change, then
legislation to actually put that into effect would have to follow.
Although New Zealand First is usually in favour of referendums of this kind, on
matters that the people should de cide, as I have already said on this occasion the people
will not in these referendums actually be deciding themselves, because the Government
has got it the wrong way around. Before spending millions of dollars on the two
referendums planned, there should be only one referendum before any panels are
appointed or other expenses are incurred. The one referendum should start out by
simply asking a simple question: do you want a new national flag to replace the current
one? That is all we need to ask for a sta rt. That should be the question. That is the
primary question, and that is the one that is being asked second in these two
referendums and it should be first. And only if the answer is yes should we spend
money on taking the matter any further. In actual f act, as Phil Goff has said, you could
have both questions asked in one referendum, but this Government wants a double
diversion and to double the cost. How silly can you get?
The process set out in this bill appears to be a way of the Government rigging t he
result, actually influencing the public and making sure that the public do what the
Government says. I do not think they will anyway, but this is what the Government is
trying to do. It is trying to pre -empt the real question, which is “Do New Zealander s
want a new flag or not?”, by producing four flags that other people have chosen to be
thrust upon New Zealanders. It is a back to front process. It is a blatant means of trying
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2231
to influence the result. It is trickery, but Kiwis will see through it. It is  transparently
clear that the Government and Mr Key are out of touch with what Kiwis want. This is
not what they want. There are a lot of things they do want, as I have said, but this is not
anywhere near a priority for the great majority of New Zealanders.
In addition to that, no detailed information has been given to people about the full
cost. The first $26 million will be just the beginning. There will be many, many more
costs amounting to tens of millions of dollars after that because we will need to not just
change flags on official places and also all military flags at embassies overseas and for
the armed forces but pay many other costs of official publications and emblems. Even
drivers’ licences and, especially, passports will have to be changed to catch up with the
changes. So the real costs have not been identified and are huge. That money is better
spent elsewhere on new homes, on education, and on better health services, including
New Zealand First’s new bill to give SuperGold cardholders three free doctors visits per
year. The people who will get that would much rather have it than a new flag, I am sure.
There is also another very important reason for us to oppose this bill, and this is that
it will betray the men and women who fought and died under this flag, our flag, in many
wars. We had 100,000 men go to the First World War from New Zealand and 18,000 of
them died—not under the flag, as one speaker said, but they were buried under the flag.
The respect that the current flag generates througho ut the world will be lost because the
new flag will take decades upon decades to even be recognised. Our current flag is
rooted in history and that history needs to be respected and preserved. We need not
adopt some fad—the fad of design this year or next year—for New Zealand’s flag. We
have a wonderful flag, which is respected, which is recognised, and which is New
Zealand’s flag. It does not need redesigning. Everybody knows it. Everybody respects
it. What else could you possibly want from a flag? What ar e we going to gain from a
new one, apart from the expenditure of a lot of money just to make one party feel better
and to try to divert people from the real issues? This is not just “a flag of historical
significance”, as it will become if this bill is pas sed—because that is what it says it will
do—it will really mean that this flag will be lost to us for ever.
There is no genuine or significant public pressure for this change of flag, nor for the
flawed process to be followed. Instead, there are much more  important constitutional
issues for us to be looking at, such as the Māori seats, a written constitution, the size of
Parliament and the size of electorates, the length of the parliamentary term, the Māori
electoral option and participation, and the role of the Treaty of Waitangi. Those are all
genuine constitutional matters that are urgent, but what is the Government doing about
them? All it has said as a result of the recent review is “Let the conversation continue.”,
or, in other words, “Let’s do nothing about all of that. Instead, let’s have a diversion just
to change the flag.” That is not good enough and New Zealand First will not
countenance it.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: I am pleased to stand and  take a call on the New
Zealand Flag Referendums Bill in its first reading. Yes, it has been rather entertaining
listening to the member from across the way over there talking about the flag. You
know, Mr O’Rourke, this is the time for you to perhaps put y our mailbox with a flag
emblem on it up for consideration, because I know that that is exactly what you would
like to do when saying that. When the National Party came into Government—

items.speaker: Denis O'Rourke
items.text: What a load of nonsense.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: —listen, listen—we made the commitment that we would hold a
binding referendum on the New Zealand flag. That is what we said we were going to do
and we are committed to doing that. We are determined to have this flag debate and we
are determined to have this referendum, so let us start by looking at everything that has
been said in the House today.
2232 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
I was quite entertained when the member Mr Goff turned round and said in this
House today that our Prime Minister, John Key, was having this fla g debate because he
wanted it to go down in history as one of his key things to do as a Prime Minister. But
Mr Goff forgets that the thing that our Prime Minister will go down in history for —one
of the many things—is that he wiped the floor with Phil Goff in 2011 when we won that
election. So that is one of the many things for which he will go down in history, in his
success as our Prime Minister.
So I just want to look at our flag because I want to say that we have had a long
history of flags in this country—changing flags, using flags, and having flags.

items.speaker: Denis O'Rourke
items.text: There is not a long history of changing flags.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: There is. I had two grandfathers who were in the Māori Pioneer
Battalion and who went to war in World War I. Yes, they went in under the Union Jack,
but when they came back, King George designed a flag to give to the Māori Pioneer
Battalion, but it was not recalled. It was called the king’s colour. It was designed and
had on it big areas of red colour that recognised the blood that was shed in the First
World War. So, you know, when you start to talk about that, that is when I am reminded
about that Māori Pioneer Battalion flag. It was one of 13 flags that were awarded to
units of the New Zealand Expeditionary Force in the First World War.
But, unfortunately, the king’s colour flag was not consecrated, presented, or paraded
because the Māori Pioneer Battalion was not recalled, as I said. So we had to wait. It
went into storage. It was put into storag e by the last commander of the battalion, and in
1939 his widow presented the king’s colour flag to the Minister of Native Affairs back
then, hoping that it would be used for the 28 th Māori Battalion. If you look at a few
articles around that, you will find that that flag lay in the museum until 1988, when the
last commander of the 28 th Māori Battalion, Sir James Hēnare, and others looked for it
and brought it back. It was consecrated in 1993.

items.speaker: Denis O'Rourke
items.text: It’s not a flag.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: This is all relevant to a flag referendum. It is all relevant. Look
at your speaking notes, Mr O’Rourke, if you have any. We are lucky to have some.
Let us have a look  at the Māori flag —OK—the Confederation of the United Tribes
of Aotearoa. In 1834, 25 chiefs from the far north were called to Waitangi—

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I beg your pardon. I a m sorry, I
am having real trouble hearing the member who is speaking at the moment and I
wonder whether you could ask the House to quieten down and allow her to speak.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Well, I am a judge of that. So long
as I can hear —[Interruption] Order! So long as I can hear what is being said; I am the
judge of that. But I do ask that the barracking across the cross benches should be lower
than that and I ask Jo Hayes to continue.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. I do not like yelling in the
House either, to be heard. As I say, in 1834, 25 chiefs from the far north gathered in
Waitangi to choose a flag to represent New Zealand. This flag was actually initiated by
James Busby—are we all listening? That meeting included 10 British commanders; so it
was not just 25 chiefs sitting at the table. There were 10 British commanders and
personnel from three American ships who attended that occasion.
So the 25 chiefs chose out of the designs the Methodist one, which became the flag
of the Confederation of the United Tribes of Aotearoa, and everybody knows that one
because it is on a white backing. The Union Jack, as we all know, came into being post
the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi, yet we still keep that Confederation of the United
Tribes flag for the iwi. New Zealand uses six other flags —there are six other flags we
use. We have the Queen’s personal flag, we use the Governor-General’s flag—

items.speaker: Denis O'Rourke
items.text: We use one.
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2233

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: These are all for occasions, Mr O’Rourke. We use the New
Zealand red ensign, which was adopted in 1903 for merchant ships. These are all flags
that signal great things that have happened in the history of this country and its
development. We use the New Zealand white ensign, which is the British one. We use
the Royal New Zealand Air Force ensign and the New Zealand civil air ensign. Then, of
course, there is the plethora of flags that iwi use. I am from the Whan ganui River and
when I go up into Ngāti Rangi —you want to see the plethora of flags that they fly.
These are the flags and some of them have the little ensign that shows British rule, but
most of them are ensigns that represent their history, so this is very important to them as
well.
What I also want to say is that my grandfathers —yes, they fought under two flags;
they did do that, but I can stand here and argue that they would not have refused to fight
because of the colour of the flag, the shape of the flag. They went over there because
they represented this country. They fought for our freedom; that is what they fought for.
They fought for our freedom so our grandchildren can live in a world that is peaceful.
That is what I can say and there is nobody i n this House or outside this House who
would refuse to do that because of the debate over this flag today—no, they would not.
As I am saying, this whole debate around the flag is a good debate. It is the
referendum that this Government said we would do and we are doing it. We are doing
it, we are listening, we will be listening, and it is all laid out within the bill.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: No, no, no, you’re not going to listen.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Mr Mark, you can sit over there and you can say “No, no, no,
no.”, but we will be listening. I am sure that if my grandfathers were alive today they
would be saying to me: “Mokopuna, make sure that we have this flag, so that when an
Australian Prime Minister goes overseas he is not welcomed by a flag that is New
Zealand’s flag, because people cannot tell the difference between the Australian flag
and the New Zealand flag.” It was written up in the media that that was what had
happened. We want a flag that is representative of all of us and it is going to be  the
people’s choice as to how we do that and how that happens. I mean to say, it is
shameful when another Prime Minister goes into a foreign country and that country has
the New Zealand flag to welcome him.
So when you sit here in this House and say that everybody knows our flag, they do
not know our flag. We need a flag that resembles who we are, so that everybody in this
world can see that we are Kiwi, we are the silver fern —we are all of those things. We
need a flag that when it is raised will send chills up people’s spines and will bring tears
not only to those watching the flag go up but to those who are watching them. That is
the type of flag we need. We need a flag that tells the world that we are Aotearoa New
Zealand. That is what we need. We need a flag where we can all stand proud and
nobody in the whole globe is going to be confused over where it comes from.
When I listened to the member of the Greens Kennedy Graham talk about the
Canadian maple leaf, everybody knows that. That is the type of thing we need so people
of this globe know where we come from. They need to know that the flag represents
people who are strong, independent, and believe in freedom. That is the type of flag we
are looking at and we need a flag that represents pure New Zealand because that is what
we are—ake ake ake, āmine, I tell you now.
In closing, I strongly urge all New Zealanders to take the opportunity to participate in
this referendum. Do not sit back—participate in it. Participate in it and have your say,
because that is what we have asked for. We are committed to that as a Government and
we are going to continue to drive that. I am very proud to stand here today and
commend this bill to the House and I also urge everybody throughout Aotearoa New
Zealand watching this debate to please participate. Kia ora.
2234 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. James
Shaw—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JAMES SHAW
items.text: A number of people who have spoken before in this
debate have mentioned the level of public interest in this issue, and the fact that the
House of Representatives is fairly empty for this debate is actually  quite representative
of the level of public interest. So this is one of those occasions where interest in the
House does seem to roughly represent the level of interest outside it.
My personal view as a modern New Zealander is that we do need to change o ur flag
and that we need a flag that tells all of our stories. In general, the Green Party supports
the idea of a public referendum to adopt a new flag that better represents the more
independent and multicultural identity of present day New Zealand. We do want the
public to have a say on this issue, and we will be supporting the bill’s referral to a select
committee.
There are three points that I would like to make about this bill, however. First of all, I
would like to say, as my colleague Dr Kennedy Graham indicated, that the flag has long
been regarded as an antiquated relic of empire. Although between 1840 and 1902 the
Union Jack was the official flag of New Zealand, the current flag was gazetted in 1869
and used aboard New Zealand ships. In 1902 a sta tute instituted the current design as
the official flag of New Zealand on land and sea. This flag’s design reflects a desire to
identify New Zealand as a self -governing but essentially still British colony in
nationality, culture, and outlook. Does anyone here think that New Zealanders today
still think of themselves as British? I say this as a proud Kiwi who was born and raised
in this country and is also a naturalised British citizen.
The New Zealand of 2015 is a multicultural, independent society, and our links with
Britain are more economic than cultural. Having lived in the United Kingdom for the
better part of 13 years, it is very clear to me that our countries are extremely different.
Although it is clear that we still have family, historical, and cu ltural relationships with
that country, we are a different country. According to the 2013 census, 12 percent of the
New Zealand population identifies as Asian and that number is expected to grow in the
next few decades. Twelve percent of our population ide ntifies as Māori, but our current
flag ignores the indigenous people of this land. If a flag is supposed to be a symbol of
national identity, the current flag is inadequate.
The second thing I would like to say is that we do have concerns about the propos ed
process that has been outlined in the bill. Having two referendums is costly and
unnecessary. The Government argued against the citizens initiated referenda on asset
sales last year on the basis of cost —that it was costly and unnecessary —and now it is
giving us two referenda on a flag rather than on the economic direction of the country.
The Government is proposing having one referendum to determine a viable alternative
before having a second, first -past-the-post, referendum between the alternative and t he
current flag. In our view it would be much cheaper to simply have one preferential
voting referendum between the current flag and a number of alternatives.
Other countries’ experiences suggest alternate approaches that the Government might
consider. In Canada the Maple Leaf Flag, which has been referred to as one of the more
successful changes of flag, was adopted in 1965 after the country’s Prime Minister
formed a committee to consider the flag question. In Jamaica Parliament approved a
new flag on the  recommendation of a special committee that had sifted through public
submissions.
The third and final point that I would like to make is that there is a need for a wider
constitutional debate and that we are putting the cart before the horse in looking a t the
symbol of our country. As this Government moves into its third term its focus on
populist gestures over meaningful reform is becoming ever more apparent. Instead of
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2235
tackling broader questions about the constitution, the Prime Minister is attempting to
distract the public with a flag debate. As I said previously, we support the principle of
changing the flag but we would prefer that to be part of a broader debate, not a political
stunt.
For instance, the Government could tackle electoral reform. The E lectoral
Commission recommended changes to MMP after the 2011 referendum, but the
Government refused to enact them because it wanted to protect its support partners.
There was a constitutional review in which a huge amount of extremely good work was
done, and that, similarly, has gone to ground. One other question is: should we remain a
constitutional monarchy or should we have a Kiwi head of State? What are the
prospects for greater Māori autonomy or self -governance? We do not pretend to have a
monopoly on wisdom regarding those issues—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry —the member’s
time has expired. I call Marama Fox—5 minutes.

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: I am also pleased to be part of the
cross-parliamentary team that has been established to engage with this issue of the New
Zealand flag, to ensure the debate has integrity and that we put in place a process to
create public confidence in the nature of the debate.
I want to remind us all not to duplicate the process that was spearheaded by the
Māori Party in 2009, where a national conversation was held about the preference of the
people for a Māori flag. In July and August 2009, 21 public hui were held across the
motu and it came down to a matter of four flags —the New Zealand flag, the New
Zealand red ensign, the United Tribes of New Zealand flag, and the tino rangatiratanga
flag. For those who do not know that flag, that wa s the flag carried during the hīkoi to
Parliament on that auspicious day, 5 May 2004. We will never forget that incredible
sight when the forecourt was filled with tino rangatiratanga flags —just saying. But the
pathway to tino rangatiratanga was seen not only in the red, white, and black colours. At
the time of our consultation process in 2009, kaumātua Matiu Tarawa, a fine 85 years
old, said that he had supported the flag of the  He Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o
Nū Tīreni for some 70 years. He saw it as the tuakana to all flags—the elder sibling.
What I loved about the comment from Matiu is the pride and the passion that he had
for the flag that he thought most denoted his nationhood. I feel much the same way
about the concept of a new national anthem, for example. I would love to engage in
discussion around the motu about what we might consider would best represent the
diverse voices of this land. As a result of the national consultation process championed
by the Māori Par ty, a Māori flag will fly alongside whatever flag is eventually chosen,
to recognise the partnership that the Crown and Māori entered into when signing Te
Tiriti o Waitangi. As a result of that process in 2009 the national Māori flag flies from
the Aucklan d Harbour Bridge, Premier House, and any other significant sites on
Waitangi Day.
Is this a necessary step at this expense, and is it worth it? I have come to the House to
fight for those who suffer hardship and disparity. For me, I would relish the chance to
vote for a flag that recognises my duality of nationhood. The first symbol of nationhood
recognised around the world should reflect our duality of nationhood. It is the tip of the
iceberg of what else we might, could, and should address to address inequality and
recognition of our place in this country. Let us be clear: the Māori Pa rty has celebrated
momentous occasions throughout its time in this House, one of which was when we
travelled to the United Nations Human Rights Council and Dr Pita Sharples signed the
Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in April 2010. Article 3 of the

items.speaker: Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples  states
items.text: “Indigenous peoples have the
right to self -determination. By virtue of that right they freely determine their political
2236 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development .” Today, as we
debate the New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill, I think back to the Declaration on the
Rights of Indigenous Peoples, which New Zealand is now a proud signatory to. I firmly
believe that the placement of equal weighting between the Māori flag and the flag that
will emerge out of this process of the referendum is an excellent way in which we can
enhance relationships between tino rangatiratanga and kāwanatanga as provided for in
Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
On that basis, the Māori Party stands to support this first reading through to the select
committee process to receive submissions to hear what the rest of New Zealand thinks.
Again, it is the tip of the iceberg. It is the beginning of recognising duality of
nationhood. Yes, it is a great expense, but it is an expense that will, hopefully, be the
beginning of addressing a number of inequalities and disparities in our country. For this
reason, we support the New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill to the select committee
process. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I am delighted to take
part in this debate, because I think it is important to nail down a few particular issues.
First of all, this is not the  silver bullet, the be all and end all, or the change that will
make us the biggest, wealthiest nation in the world, but it is, actually, an important step
along the way to nationhood. We need to understand we were a little colony at the
bottom of the Sout h Pacific. We called her “Mother England”. She literally took all of
our goods and services, and we were more British than you could get. Michael Joseph
Savage’s famous speech in 1939 was: “Where Britain goes, we go. Where Britain
stands, we stand.”
Well, that is no longer true. That is no longer true. They cut the apron strings. They
kicked us out like a teenager gets kicked out of home. They did not even give us a bit of
spending money to go. I have to say I am a bit down and dirty on the way the Poms got
rid of us. They just gave us the boot. But that is fine. We have had to find new markets.
We have had to become a country in our own right. And guess what? Of recent times,
brand New Zealand is getting to be so important around the world. There is stuff that
Peter Jackson has done, stuff that our wine industry is doing, and stuff that is value -
added to some of our technology, our dairy, and our meat products and so on. Brand
New Zealand is getting to be more and more important, so I think it is well overdue for
us to look, as a nation, at what our symbol is. Obviously, one of the symbols of your
nationhood is your flag.
So to those who are worried about the changing of the flag, let us go through a few
things. First of all, the flag we have currently got is not New Zealand’s first one. It is
not our first flag. Actually, until 1902 it was the Union Jack. That was our flag. Let us
just make sure that everyone understands what the Union Jack is. It is a combination of
three sets of crosses: St David of Wales , St George of England, and St Andrew of
Scotland. How does that have any relationship to us at the bottom of the South Pacific?
How does a Union Jack have any relationship to us at all? It does not.
The next thing I think is worth telling —and this is act ually a true story Don
McKinnon told us once in Cabinet. He was our foreign Minister, and he attended a big
United Nations function, I think, and so on. All the foreign Ministers were asked to
come up, pick their flag out of a big rotunda thing, go and pla ce it in these holders, and
then stand underneath it. It was done alphabetically, so when McKinnon went up, he
was about halfway through, as “n” for New Zealand. Our flag was not there. Don

items.speaker: McKinnon went
items.text: “Uh oh.” Then he suddenly spotted the Australian fl ag was still there.
Gareth Evans, the then foreign Minister of Australian, when he had walked up, had
gone up, picked our flag, and gone and stuck it up, not realising he had got the wrong
flag. So that is how similar they are. Why the hell our stars are r ed and theirs are white
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2237
no one has ever been able to tell me. Other than that, that is the only way I can spot the
difference. They have got white stars; we have got red ones. They have got a bigger
one, but it is hardly that much of a difference. Frankly,  we want to be a nation in our
own right. So I give absolutely full credit to the Prime Minister for saying it is time we
began a process of identifying ourselves as a nation and having a symbol that represents
it.
I want to make it clear that a whole lot of my family members served. My father and
his brother served on the HMNZS Achilles  at the Battle of the River Plate, two of his
other brothers served in the New Zealand Army in the desert, and two of them served in
the air force in part of the Battle of Britain. I do not believe any one of them, who have
all passed on, would say: “I served under a particular flag, so I want that flag kept.” You
know why they served? They served against the tyranny of—in that particular case—the
Nazis and what they were do ing in the world, and they served for New Zealand. They
served for their country and for the people of this country, in order to keep it safe. The
piece of linen that might have been fluttering above them on one day is not what they
did it for. They did it for their nation and their people, to keep them safe and secure.
I have got a feeling that a lot of old soldiers, many of whom have passed, would be
very happy for us to be now moving to the idea of a different flag that stood out and that
was us—a flag that is New Zealand and that is us, so when we go on the world stage,
everyone does not go: “Oh, is that the Australian flag? No.” There are a number of other
nations that have got the Union Jack sitting up in their top left -hand corner, and
everyone is saying: “Ah, what country is that again?”. It would be great.
Again, we have heard about Canada and the maple leaf. What a stunningly good
example of change. Ask any Canadian —please do, because I have done it —whether
they would go back. Ask any Canadian whe ther they would like to go back to their old
flag. It is not even up for discussion. The maple leaf is now hoisted and they feel proud
of it. It gives them some identity. It is their nation. It is not the same as anybody else’s.
That is what I would love to see happen.
I do not have a particularly strong view about the design, other than a couple of
things. I would like it to be as simple as it can be, because kids like to draw flags. You
want to stick a flag on the side of your car when your rugby team is  playing, so please
do not make it so you have to be an artist of greatness and spend 3 hours drawing all the
fancy bits to make it work. It should be something quite simple. In the case of the maple
leaf, you can flick your hand around and draw the maple leaf within a couple of
seconds, and that is it, on a plain background. Just make it that it is a New Zealand icon
that we can all be proud of and that can be put on products that we sell around the
world, or we can wear it as part of our sporting teams.

items.speaker: I make this point
items.text: when we see the All Blacks go to the Rugby World Cup and we
are cheering them on, are they wearing the Union Jack? Come on! Have a look at any
rugby stadium and see whether the kids are out there waving the Union Jack to support
the All Blacks. They are not. They are out there waving the silver fern because, at least
at this point, until we get this flag thing sorted, it is the closest thing we can get to our
nationhood. How awful would it be if we were up against the Poms in the final of  the
Rugby World Cup and we are waving a flag with the Union Jack on it? We would not
do it.
So it is not our first flag. We have changed it in the past. I do not accept the argument
that people, because they fought under it and died—and many hundreds of thousands
along the way have given their lives in that service —do not want to see that change
now. In fact, I think the point has been made already that on many of our war graves
around the world the silver fern is above every one of the commemorative litt le plaques
for each of the soldiers —the silver fern is, not the Union Jack with a couple of stars on
2238 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
the bottom of it. So this is a really important step forward for us as a nation and for
where we go from here, and I am delighted that we are taking it.
To those members from the Labour Party —and I have heard a few of them getting
stuck into this Government and saying: “Ah, you know, you’re boxing forward with this
without the consent of the people.” —I want to say that they took some much bigger
constitutional issue changes of this country than the flag, with no consultation
whatsoever and not to an election. What are they? Well, let us go through them. How
about we take getting rid of the Privy Council? I support it. I am not criticising them. I
actually think that the time to cut the strings with the Privy Council was well overdue. I
support it. But Labour just boxed on and got rid of it. It threw the Privy Council out.
That is it. There was no referendum, there was no consultation, and it was not part of a n
election referendum —done. It was similar with our knighthood honours and so on.
Labour decided that it did not like the knights and the dames, that it was just going to
change all of that—bang, done, did not consult on it, and so on. So it is a bit rich when
some people come into this House and say “Oh, you haven’t consulted with us.” or
“You’re not taking account of this.”, when those Labour members alone went out and
sort of banged things through.
I want to finally say to New Zealanders that this is not massive. This is not the game-
changer that will see us be the economic powerhouse to take on the world, but it is a
really important element of our becoming a nation. It is a really important part of us
being an entity in the rest of the world, and I wou ld love to think that we ended up with
a flag—and, as I said before, I do not have any preconceived ideas on it —that when
New Zealanders are travelling they will have on their backpacks, or have on their shirts.
When we are at rugby matches and we see that  flying, or we see it at the —someone
actually showed me a clip the other day of a couple of Commonwealth Games medal
ceremonies. The flags were all going up in the air. All three had Union Jacks and one
had some red stars and one had some white stars, and you could not work out whether
the Australians had got the gold or whether it was the New Zealanders who got the gold.
If anyone from overseas was looking at it, they would say: “Oh, that country cleaned up
on all three.”
So it has to be different. It has  to be unique. I agree with a couple of the people
speaking from the perspective of Māoridom. It would be great if we could include
something like the koru that Air New Zealand has done, something that is uniquely
Māori as part of it. I would love to see t hat. But, in the end, this country deserves to
have a stake in the ground that people around the world recognise. It goes with our pride
as a nation as we go forward.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call will be a split call.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: What a load of absolute bollocks! If that
member thinks that a flag defines who we are as a country, then that represents the
greatest level of colonial insecurity that I have come across in a long time. I tell you
what, a flag never defines how I view ou r country. Mr Williamson talked about his
ancestors who had served this country. He talked about the fact that they did not stand
under a piece of linen. Well, I have had several members of my family who have put a
hell of a lot of service into this country and if they thought for one moment that we were
prioritising a flag over child poverty, over unemployment, over economic development,
then they would actually roll in their graves. This is an absolute disgrace.
Mr Williamson said that we need something that we can take overseas and be proud
of. Well, for me, I would be a hell of a lot prouder if I could go overseas as a Kiwi and
say: “You know what? In New Zealand there is no child poverty. In New Zealand there
is no unemployment, and there is no Governm ent debt.” But we cannot say those things
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2239
at all. In fact, all three of those are just examples of the absolute disgrace that this
Government has presided over for the last 7 years.
I get quite riled up about this because when I hear people say that a fla g is what
defines us as a nation, I think how ridiculous. If New Zealanders think we are that
shallow, then heaven help us. I know that the vast majority of people whom I talk to and
whom I associate with are not that shallow in any way, shape, or form.
What I would like to talk about in the next 4 minutes is the actual process. The thing
I like doing when I look at these bills is going through the regulatory impact statement,
because what the regulatory impact statement is supposed to be is a rather objec tive
view of how the bill is going to impact on New Zealanders, written by Government
officials who are not supposed to be in the pocket of the Government but who provide
the Government with advice and the members on the select committee with a way
forward in things they need to consider.

items.speaker: The first thing this says is
items.text: “Any process considering change must be robust in that it
needs to lead to a legitimate outcome which is accepted by the public.” We all agree on
that. That is vitally important. But then we go through this and it says: “A number of
decisions have been made by Cabinet limiting the focus of the [regulatory impact
statement].” So, immediately, the Ministry of Justice has said: “OK, well, we can’t
consider a whole lot of options because the Cabinet has said so.” Then it says: “We
have not considered status quo as a feasible option due to decisions already made by
Cabinet.”—already made by Cabinet. So, immediately, what we have got are decisions
made by Cabinet that are going to influence this whole process.

items.speaker: Then we have got here
items.text: “We have not considered holding a ballot together with a
general election due to the Prime Minister’s indication that the process should be
completed before the 2017 General Election.” So, yet again, we have got the Prime
Minister dictating this whole process. This is not going to be accepted by the public as a
legitimate outcome.
Why this process? If it is done in a general election, we get about 80 percent turnout.
You are going to get the majority of Kiwis who are goin g to vote because they go to the
polling booth anyway. The history of postal ballots is around about 50 percent, the
absolute maximum, so we are not going to get the vast majority of Kiwis engaging in
this. In fact, it says “we might expect” —we might—“that  consideration of the New
Zealand Flag is an issue New Zealanders will find engaging. This could mean higher
voter turnout,” —in a postal poll —“as long as the referendum is well -timed and the
question(s) well-framed.” If that is not an official saying: “This is not a very good idea
but we can’t say that because we don’t want to annoy Cabinet”, then I do not know
what is.
This is a process that is being driven by Cabinet and the Prime Minister in a way that
I actually believe is possibly —well, if it is not u nconstitutional, then it is certainly
unfair. If we really do want to change the flag, if New Zealanders really do want a
change, then make it easy —as this document says it has to be. In fact, in this statement
it actually outlines the fact that public acc essibility on the option put forward by the
Government—it says it is medium. Public accessibility means “a referendum process
that is easy to understand and participate in, where voters understand the implications of
their vote.” And the Ministry of Justic e says that is not that high. New Zealanders will
not engage. Thank you.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. It actually
is a privilege to speak on this bill, the New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill, proposed by
the Hon Bill English, and I do so acknowledging that this is the beginning of the end of
the $3.9 million constitutional conversation that Bill English oversaw. In fact, what was
really interesting about that constitutional conversation is that Mr English said that i f
2240 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 12 Mar 2015
there was to be any significant change it would “require either broad cross -party
agreement or the majority su pport of voters at  a referendum.” So the mandate for this
piece of legislation comes from the “other issues” section of the recommendations of
that constitutional conversation that said “ the role and functions of the Head of State
and symbols of state ”—I presume that is where the mandate for this comes from, from
Bill English’s perspective.

items.speaker: The reality of the question
items.text: “Are you in favour of changing the New Zealand
flag?”—actually, New Zealanders have been asked that question. On 27 September last
year, in a poll of over 1,000 voters on One News, 65 percent of New Zealanders said no.
On 25 February 2014 they had also been asked that question—this was a bit earlier in
the process—and 72 percent said no. And if we look at 2004, which was 10 years ago,
58 percent said no. So maybe there was a little bit of a window in 2004, and that was on
the end of the Don Brash Ōrewa speech and the foreshore and seabed legislation.
But what I want to contribute is that, in fact, the flag that we are discussing today is
actually the third flag this country has had. The first flag, actually, was the flag of the
United Tribes of Aotearoa. On 20 March 1834, 25 chiefs in New Zealand asserted our
sovereignty as a nation for the very first time. That was our first flag. On 6 Februa ry
1840 our flag changed again, and it did become the Union Jack. Guess why? We signed
a treaty with the British, so New Zealand became part of the British Empire . The flag
that we have today we actually adopted under the New Zealand Ensign and Code
Signals Bill of 1902, in recognition of the 6,500 New Zealanders who went and fought
in the Boer War between 1899 and 1902. It was a very significant event because it was
the first time as a country we had actually asserted ourselves internationally, not as
British citizens, but actually as New Zealand citizens.
So, significant events have happened for us to look at our flag, and my question is:
has a significant incident happened for us to be debating this today? It is going to cost
the country $26 million and, as my colleague Stuart Nash pointed out, we have got a
whole lot of other things that we would rather spend $26 million on. So for the
Government to make this its priority, I guess we are a bit dumbfounded on this side of
the House.
So why change the flag? Actually, there has been a history of MPs wanting to change
the flag. In 1979 National MP Allan Higget—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Highet.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Highet—thank you, Grant. Thank you, I was worried about that
pronunciation. He was the Minister of Internal Affairs. He wanted to change the flag,
and guess what happened? There was no interest —no interest in changing the flag. In
1988 Labour MP Russell Marshall, who was the Minister of Foreign Affairs, mooted a
change to the flag. Did New Zealanders support him? Of course they did not. In 1992
the leader of Mana Motuhake, Matiu Rata, a former Minister of Māori Affairs, mooted a
change to the flag. For hi m it was about our indigenous culture and our indigenous
identity. In 1998 National MP Marie Hasler, Minister of Cultural Affairs, wanted to
change the flag. No traction —no one wanted to do it. In 2004 Lloyd Morrison started
the NZFlag.com Trust and he wanted to initiate a citizens initiated referendum to
change the flag. Only 100,000 New Zealanders signed that petition. It needed 270,000
signatures, so it failed.
And today we have National MP John Key, who is the Minister of Tourism, the
Minister for National Security and Intelligence, and the Minister responsible for
Ministerial Services—he wants to change the flag. If he really wants to change the flag,
why does he not go through a citizens initiated referendum? He needs only 330,000
signatures to do tha t, but what is he doing? He is using the privilege of being in
Government to push this through, and I think it is absolutely appalling at a time when
12 Mar 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 2241
child poverty is what it is. For this Government to abuse that power is absolutely
disgusting. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak on
the first reading of the New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill. I am not on the Justice and
Electoral Committee, which has been given this bill, so it is a real privilege for me to be
able to make this contribution to the bill. I acknowledge the Deputy Prime Minister, Bill
English, as the Minister responsible for the flag consideration process, and I
acknowledge the work tha t the Deputy Prime Minister, Bill English, has put into this
bill.
What we are hearing from the other side tells us about their lack of a futuristic
approach. They do not believe in giving a fair opportunity to Kiwis to contribute to this
issue. We know t hat this issue is not a new issue. This debate has come up many times
before, since the 1970s, so it is time that we give Kiwis a formal and respectful platform
